\title{Ordered energy gaps and actual decreasing-net closure\\
on a nonalgebraizable analytic surface}
\author{Independent scoped proof draft; unverified}
\date{9 October 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
We reconstruct the continuous and decreasing-generated Monge--Ampere
calculus on a particular proper, genuinely nonalgebraizable analytic
surface, including point atoms, full pointwise generated uniqueness,
finite scalar extension, and fixed bounded curvature probes. We then
prove a quantitative ordered energy-gap estimate. It shows that every
energy-bounded decreasing net of actual generated weights has an actual
continuous decreasing sequence presentation, without a countable
cofinality assumption. Its energy, Monge--Ampere measures, mixed products
and moving moments are continuous in the directed order. For each
arbitrary-support finite-full-dual measure there is also actual ordered
net $L^1$ convergence. These results do not prove compactness of arbitrary
normalized energy-sublevel nets, obstacle orthogonality or arbitrary-measure
existence. The unchanged original P16.7 remains unresolved.
\end{abstract}

\section{Carrier, positivity and conventional foundations}
Set $K=\mathbb C((s))$, $|s|=e^{-1/8}$, $t=s^8$, and
\[
Y=(\mathbb G_m^2)^{\rm an}_K,\quad
\Lambda=\langle(t,2),(3,t)\rangle,\quad X=Y/\Lambda,
\qquad \tau=(-\log|z_1|,-\log|z_2|).
\]
The valuation translations of the two generators are the standard basis
of $\mathbb Z^2$. Tropical rectangles of widths less than one have
disjoint nonidentity translates and give ordinary open injective charts.
The compact polyannulus $\tau^{-1}([0,1]^2)$ covers the quotient.
On bounded boxes only finitely many closed deck graphs meet. A finite
union of injective charts is a flat quasi-finite surjection with finite
fibres; descent of the relation's coherent ideal makes the diagonal
closed. This uses Conrad--Temkin Lemmas 4.2.3--4.2.4: local quotients of
an etale relation on an ordinary open cover glue to the analytic quotient,
and coherent G-sheaves descend along flat quasi-finite analytic
surjections. The latter is used on the finite chart cover, never on the
infinite-sheeted map $Y\to X$. Thus $X$ is compact, separated, good,
strict, smooth, connected, boundaryless and pure of dimension two.
Strict affinoid neighbourhoods follow from rational radii in the divisible
value group. Compactness and absence of boundary give properness.

Here is a direct nonalgebraization argument, with its algebraic and
analytic foundations stated. Gruson IV.5 Theorem 1 says that completed
products of disc algebras with radii in the divisible value group and
unit-circle algebras have $SK^0=0$. Taking determinants trivializes
rank-one projective modules on these products. For a wide annulus,
trivialize its line bundle on the inner circle times the other factors,
glue to a trivial bundle on the inner disc, and fill to the outer disc.
Tate--Kiehl coherent gluing, in Van der Put 2.14--2.16.3, applies to this
finite rational cover, whose intersection is the inner circle. Induction
on the wide annulus factors gives
\[
\operatorname{Pic}(P_m)=0,
\quad P_m=\{|s|^m\le |z_i|\le |s|^{-m},\ i=1,2\}.
\]
This does not apply Gruson's theorem directly to wide annuli.
For a unit $b=\sum b_\beta z^\beta$ on $P_m$, its Gauss log norm and
the opposite log norm of its inverse are convex, so its log norm is
affine. A maximizing monomial at an interior point agrees with that
affine norm throughout the box. For its exponent $\alpha$,
\[
|b_\beta/b_\alpha|\exp((m/8)|\beta-\alpha|_1)\le1.
\]
Hence $b=b_\alpha z^\alpha(1+g)$ and
$\|g\|_{P_j}\le |s|^{m-j}$ for $j<m$. Consecutive frames can be
normalized by scalar monomials so their transition is $1+g_m$.
On every fixed $P_j$ the products of these transitions and inverse tails
converge. Correcting the frames by these products gives a global frame,
and therefore $\operatorname{Pic}(Y)=0$. A global analytic unit on $Y$
is a scalar monomial: a second exponent would dominate along a tropical
ray and contradict global affinity of the Gauss log norm.

Deck multipliers of a line bundle pulled to $Y$ are $c_i z^{h_i}$.
Write $h_1=(A,B)$, $h_2=(C,D)$. The cocycle condition is
$t^C2^D=3^At^B$, so $C=B$, $A=D=0$ and
$h_1=(0,k)$, $h_2=(k,0)$. If $k\ne0$, take
$\lambda=\lambda_1\lambda_2^{\operatorname{sign}k}$; its exponent
$h=(k\operatorname{sign}k,k)$ satisfies $v(\lambda^h)=2|k|>0$.
For a section $f(\lambda z)=cz^hf(z)$ its nonzero coefficient orbit is
\[
a_{m+jh}=a_m c^j\lambda^{-jm-hj(j+1)/2}.
\]
Its valuations have negative quadratic leading term, impossible for a
Laurent series convergent on the unit polyannulus. If $k=0$, two nonzero
exponents would differ by $(p,q)$ with $t^p2^q=3^pt^q=1$;
valuation and then constants force $p=q=0$. Thus each nonzero section
is a nowhere-zero monomial and sections with the same multipliers are
proportional.

For a meromorphic function $F$ the pole ideal
$J=\{b:bF\text{ is analytic}\}$ is a coherent invertible ideal:
locally it is the kernel of multiplication by a numerator into the
quotient by a denominator; regular local factoriality makes this kernel
principal, and flat analytic restriction preserves it. The conventional
inputs are Stacks 0AG0 (a regular local ring is a UFD) and Ducros,
\emph{Families of Berkovich spaces} 2.1.3(2),(5) and 2.1.4 (the
relevant affinoid/analytic-local restrictions and algebraic-to-analytic
local maps are regular). Trivialize $J$ on $Y$. Its frame and its product
with $F$ are sections with the same deck multipliers. Hence
$\Gamma(X,\mathscr M_X)=K$.
If $X=Z^{\rm an}$ for a separated finite-type algebraic space,
Conrad--Temkin Theorem 2.3.1 reflects separatedness, smoothness and
properness. Smooth connected $Z$ is integral of dimension two.
Stacks 086U supplies a dense scheme locus for a decent space, 0BB1
supplies finiteness of the generic points on quasi-compact etale charts,
and 0EN6, 0ENA, 0END identify its rational and meromorphic function
field. Their hypotheses (weak associates of codimension zero and
generic points represented by field monomorphisms) hold for smooth
separated finite-type $Z$. Flat analytic local maps preserve denominators;
a closed point in a scheme open detects each nonzero rational function.
Consequently $K(Z)\hookrightarrow\Gamma(X,\mathscr M_X)=K$, contrary
to $\operatorname{trdeg}_K K(Z)=2$. This proves genuine
nonalgebraizability over the stated field, without asserting it over all
extensions.

Locally put $\rho=|\tau|^2/2$ and $\theta=\DD\rho$.
Deck changes of $\rho$ are smooth affine unit logarithms. Identity-torus
calibration has saturated lattice $\mathbb Z^2$, analytic multiplicity
one and the raw factor $2!$, so $\theta^2$ is twice Lebesgue measure
on the reference Gauss section and
\[
M=\int_X\theta^2=2.
\]
No probability normalization is used. In particular $\theta$ vanishes
on residue bidiscs; reference gradient energy alone cannot separate
weights.

Let $\mathscr P$ be the minimal sheaf of finite continuous CLD psh
functions containing ordinary smooth psh functions and closed under
local uniform limits (CLD v2 Definition 8.1.7 and Lemma 8.1.8). Set
\[
\C=\{a\in C(X,\RR):\rho+a\in\mathscr P\text{ locally}\},\quad
\theta_a=\theta+\DD a,
\quad B(a,b)=\theta_a\wedge\theta_b,\quad \MA(a)=B(a,a).
\]
All continuous closure stages are retained. The published continuous
product rules used are CLD 8.5.1 (continuous multiplication and
convergence for positive currents), 8.5.3 (differentiation through smooth
closed factors), 8.5.5--6 (positivity of $\DD(fT)$ for continuous psh
$f$ and positive closed $T$, and proper projection), 8.7.1--4
(recursive products, local uniform continuity, positivity, symmetry),
8.8.4--5 (continuous dpsh extension and smooth $\DD$-null changes).
The carrier is boundaryless; all local factors are continuous dpsh or
continuous psh as required. Positive top currents are actual Radon
measures by 7.2.8, and 7.2.9--12 gives coefficient measures and positive
order-zero extension. Smooth cutoffs, partitions and scalar approximation
are supplied by 6.2.4--8 on locally differentially separated charts.
Green and Stokes are 5.11.1; boundary terms vanish here. The compatibility
of separated equidimensional analytic spaces with this tropical calculus
is 15.7.1. We do not use arbitrary-multiplier closedness in 8.6.7.
These are conventional analytic foundations, with the whole applied
immediate units recorded in the local ledger. Their deeper Berkovich,
Temkin, Ducros, Kiehl, Thuillier, graded commutative algebra and relative
intersection foundations are disclosed, not claimed freshly recursively
audited.

\section{All-stage Green calculus and bounded energy}
Convex and finite-max closure of $\C$ follows at all stages: first use
smooth convex soft maxima, then fix one slot and use the uniform-closed
sheaf/minimality argument, and repeat in the other slot. Constants are
allowed. The bounded products glue across affine reference changes and
have mass $M$ by testing exact terms with 1.

For positive closed $(1,1)$ current $T$, complete compact smooth
$(1,0)$ forms in the positive semidefinite pairing
$\int \alpha\wedge J\beta\wedge T$. For a nonnegative compact smooth
cutoff $\chi$ use the corresponding local completion. Uniformly smooth
approximable functions with strongly convergent gradients form a sheaf
$H_T$: partitions and Leibniz patch local approximants. Continuous
bounded coefficients act by approximation and
$\|f\alpha\|\le\|f\|_\infty\|\alpha\|$.
A uniformly zero sequence with a strong gradient limit has zero
gradient: by closedness it pairs to zero with every smooth Hilbert test,
since its pairing is the integral of the function against the fixed
differentiated test. These tests are dense.
If $f\in H_T$ and $L_Tf=\DD(fT)$ is signed Radon, smooth
approximation first in $f$ and then in a compactly supported $g$ gives
\[
\int g L_Tf=-Q_T(f,g),\qquad
Q_{T,\chi}(f)=\tfrac12\int f^2\DD\chi\wedge T-
\int\chi fL_Tf.
\]
The sheaf $\{f\in H_T:L_Tf\ge0\}$ contains smooth psh functions.
If such $f_j$ converge uniformly, choose nested cutoffs $\chi,\eta$,
$\eta=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, with $|f_j|\le B$ on
the entire support of $\eta$. For $\epsilon=\|f_j-f_k\|$ there,
positivity and the displayed identity give
\[
0\le Q_{T,\chi}(f_j-f_k)\le
\tfrac12\epsilon^2\|\DD\chi\wedge T\|_{\rm TV}
+2B\epsilon\|\chi\|_\infty\|\DD\eta\wedge T\|_{\rm TV}.
\]
Thus the gradients are strongly Cauchy. Choose local smooth approximants
with both uniform and gradient errors tending to zero. Positivity
survives distributional limits. Minimality includes every stage of
$\mathscr P$; differences and finite patching give, for continuous dpsh
$f,g$ on $X$,
\[
Q_T(f,g)=-\int f\DD(gT)=-\int g\DD(fT),\quad Q_T(f)\ge0.
\tag{G}
\]
This supplies strong gradients rather than an unsupported pullback of
an arbitrary current.

Define
\[
E(a)=\tfrac13\int a\,[\theta^2+B(a,0)+\MA(a)].
\]
Differentiating the cubic using (G), for $a_t=(1-t)a+tb$ gives
\[
E'(a_t)=\int(b-a)\MA(a_t),\qquad
\frac{d^2}{dt^2}E(a_t)=-2Q_{\theta_{a_t}}(b-a)\le0.
\]
Consequently $E$ is concave, monotone, $E(0)=0$,
$E(a+c)=E(a)+2c$, and tangent inequalities hold. Integrating the
quadratic Bernstein coefficients gives the cocycle
\[
E(b)-E(a)=\tfrac13\int(b-a)[\MA(a)+B(a,b)+\MA(b)].
\tag{C}
\]
If $a\le b$, every one of these positive integrals is at most
$3(E(b)-E(a))$.
For bounded comparison use $m=\max(a,b-\epsilon)$, locality on the
strict ordinary open comparison sets and equal mass. This gives
$\MA(b)\{a<b-\epsilon\}\le\MA(a)\{a\le b-\epsilon\}$;
both increasing unions as $\epsilon\downarrow0$ equal $\{a<b\}$.
Contact atoms are retained on the indicated sides.

\section{Canonical generated calculus and the full bounded dual}
Define $\G$ by actual pointwise presentations
$a_j\downarrow u$, $a_j\in\C$, $\inf_j E(a_j)>-\infty$.
All values, including poles, are actual USC representatives. The
following compact strict-domination fact will be used repeatedly:
if a decreasing net of USC functions $f_i$ has infimum $f$ and a
finite continuous $h$ satisfies $f<h$ everywhere on compact $X$,
the increasing ordinary opens $\{f_i<h\}$ cover $X$; a finite
subcover and directedness give one global late index. No psh assertion
is made about a minimum of finitely many bounds.

Compare presentations with a term of the other plus $\epsilon$ using
this fact and the constant rule. Reversing roles proves independence
of $E(u)=\lim E(a_j)$, and the same argument proves order preservation
and energy continuity whenever a decreasing generated family has an
already generated infimum. It applies to nets as well as sequences.
An identically $-\infty$ limit would eventually lie below every negative
constant, contradicting the energy bound. Finite convex combinations
are generated and concavity passes to them.

On every finite simplex of generated weights the bounded energies are
polynomials of total degree at most three. Values converge at a finite
unisolvent set, so all coefficients converge. Existence of such a set
follows since a polynomial vanishing on an open simplex is zero.
Zero-weight slots are omitted at boundary points. This is finite
polynomial interpolation, with no differentiation of an uncontrolled
infinite limit.
For $a_j\downarrow u$ and $v\in\C$, put
$P_j(t)=E((1-t)a_j+tv)$ and $R_j(t)=E(ta_j)$. First variation gives
\[
\int v\MA(a_j)=P'_j(0)+R'_j(1).
\]
Thus its limit is canonical. The span of $\C$ is a uniformly dense
vector lattice in $C(X)$. Different tropical classes are separated by
small smooth periodic perturbations. In a single fibre different
seminorms are separated by a Laurent polynomial $P$ and a small cap
$\max(\rho_a,\delta+\epsilon(\log|P|-b))-\rho_a$, zero on a
fixed tropical boundary collar and near polynomial zeros, extended by
zero. Finite maxima give the lattice identity
\[
\max(A(p-q),A(r-s))=
2A\max((p+s)/2,(r+q)/2)-A(q+s).
\]
Constants, separation and the finite-cover lattice approximation prove
density. Positive common mass extends convergence to every continuous
test. Compact Hausdorff Riesz representation gives an actual positive
Radon $\MA(u)$ of mass 2. Polarization gives actual positive canonical
mixed products $B(u,v)$, obtained from bounded analytic products.

For positive Radon $\mu$ define the FULL bounded dual
\[
E^*(\mu)=\sup_{a\in\C}(E(a)-\int a\,d\mu).
\]
Constants force $\mu(X)=2$ if this is finite. For $u\le0$,
monotone convergence from a common continuous upper bound gives
\[
\int(-u)\,d\mu\le E^*(\mu)-E(u).
\tag{D}
\]
This proves integrability and $L^1(\mu)$ convergence of presentations;
generated pole sets are $\mu$-null. Bounded tangent gives
$E^*(\MA(a))=E(a)-\int a\MA(a)$.
The coefficient $D_u=\lim\int a_j\MA(a_j)=R'(1)$ exists.
Passing bounded tangent with fixed bounded competitors first yields
$E^*(\MA(u))\le E(u)-D_u<\infty$, so integrability precedes
the use of any unbounded moving integral. For $k\ge j$, (C) gives
\[
0\le\int(a_j-a_k)\MA(a_k)\le3(E(a_j)-E(a_k)).
\]
Let $k\to\infty$ using the fixed continuous $a_j$, and then
$j\to\infty$ using the established $L^1$ convergence. It follows
that $D_u=\int u\MA(u)$ and
$E^*(\MA(u))=E(u)-\int u\MA(u)$.

The coefficient $\partial_s E(tu+sv)|_{(1,0)}$ equals
$\int v\MA(u)$. Prove this first for bounded $v$, then decrease
bounded presentations to $v$, using coefficient convergence and (D).
For ANY continuous decreasing presentations $a_j\downarrow u$,
$b_j\downarrow v$, interpolation of $E(ta_j+sb_j)$ therefore gives
all four moving moments
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\int a_j\MA(a_j)\to\int u\MA(u),&
\int b_j\MA(a_j)\to\int v\MA(u),\\
\int a_j\MA(b_j)\to\int u\MA(v),&
\int b_j\MA(b_j)\to\int v\MA(v).
\end{array}
\tag{4M}
\]
Polarization gives mixed moments and $B(p,q)\le2\MA((p+q)/2)$.
First variation and tangent inequalities consequently pass to generated
segments. Nonopen comparison and max locality follow by bounded
Lipschitz ramps: replace presentation differences by generated differences
using moving $L^1$, then by fixed continuous presentation terms using
fixed-slot $L^1$, pass weak limits, and decrease those terms. At every
atom-free level the ramps give indicator convergence; there are at most
countably many bad levels. Regular finite Borel restrictions are determined
by continuous tests. Thus
\[
\MA(v)\{u<v\}\le\MA(u)\{u<v\},\quad
1_{u>v}\MA(\max(u,v))=1_{u>v}\MA(u).
\]
For $u\le0$, $u^A=\max(u,-A)$,
$1_{u>-A}\MA(u^A)=1_{u>-A}\MA(u)$; the entire contact set
$u=-A$ is excluded. If $E(u)\ge-C$, (D) and bounded dual give discarded
mass at most $3C/A$. These generated clamps are not assumed to be
preexisting continuous CLD functions.

\section{All bounded tests and actual point atoms}
For $a,b,w\le0$ of energy at least $-C$, (C) at zero gives
$-\int q\MA(q)\le3C$ and $E^*(\MA(q))\le2C$.
Hence
\[
\int(-p)\MA(q)\le3C,\qquad
\int(-p)B(q,r)\le6C.
\tag{M}
\]
Set $f=a-b$, $g=(a+b)/2$, $h=w-g$ and
$I(a,b)=\int(a-b)(\MA(b)-\MA(a))$.
Green and symmetry give
\[
I=Q_{\theta_a}(f)+Q_{\theta_b}(f),\qquad
Q_{\theta_w}(f)-I/2=Q_{\theta_a}(f,h)-Q_{\theta_b}(f,h).
\]
The second identity has both sides $-\int f\DD f\wedge\DD h$.
Since $|h|\le-w+(-a-b)/2$, (M) bounds its MA moments by $6C$
and mixed moments by $12C$. Expanding
$Q_{\theta_a}(h)=-\int h[B(a,w)-(\MA(a)+B(a,b))/2]$
bounds this slot by $12C+3C+6C=21C$, and likewise for $b$.
Direct-sum Cauchy--Schwarz proves
\[
Q_{\theta_w}(a-b)\le I/2+\sqrt{42CI}.
\tag{T}
\]
Fixed additive shifts leave curvatures, $Q$ and $I$ unchanged.

\begin{proposition}\label{atoms}
At every point $x\in X$ of total graded dimension two there is
$w_x\in\C$ and $\alpha_x>0$ with
$\MA(w_x)\ge\alpha_x\delta_x$. Every generated weight is finite
at $x$. No ground-field extension is used to construct this atom.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
In an injective torus chart a full-dimensional point has support kernel
zero by the graded Abhyankar inequality. Its completed field is the
completion of $K(z_1,z_2)$ with the point norm. Completion adds no
initial forms: approximate a nonzero element with error smaller than its
norm. Initial Laurent polynomials generate its graded residue field by
fractions. Choose two homogeneous algebraically independent such
initials, represented by Laurent polynomials $P_1,P_2$.
With $r_i=|P_i(x)|>0$, independence makes the image of $x$ under
$(P_1,P_2)$ exactly the weighted Gauss point of radii $r_i$, including
arbitrary positive real radii. Boundarylessness places $x$ in the
relative interior. CLD 11.6.5(c) applies: both dimensions are at most
two, the image has graded dimension two and the target is reduced.
It makes the map finite and flat at $x$. By 11.6.3 take compact local
representatives of rank $D>0$ with singleton Gauss fibre $\{x\}$.
Near the target Gauss point the target's pleasant moment has plane
calibration one; CLD 14.5.2--3 gives degree $D$ upstairs.

For $\psi=\max(0,\log(|P_1|/r_1),\log(|P_2|/r_2))$, its smoothed
log-sum-exp models have plane Hessian determinant $p_0p_1p_2$ after
the corresponding scale change. The gradient map fills the open
standard simplex, of area $1/2$, so the raw $2!$ top mass is one.
The smooth measures concentrate at its vertex as the smoothing tends
to zero. Their pushforwards on the local finite representative have
mass $D$. Finite properness and the singleton Gauss fibre show convergence
against every actual continuous upstairs test to $D\delta_x$:
given a neighbourhood of $x$, shrink the target so its full inverse
image lies there, and use bounded continuous oscillation. Uniform
continuity of bounded products identifies this with $(\DD\psi)^2$
near $x$. This is an actual atom, not just its tropical pushforward.

On a small tropical box choose $\rho_a=|\tau-a|^2/2$,
$0<\delta$ smaller than the minimum of $\rho_a$ on a boundary collar,
and $\epsilon>0$ so small that
$w_x=\max(\rho_a,\delta+\epsilon\psi)-\rho_a$ is zero on that
collar. Extend by zero. At polynomial zeros use capped smooth logs
which are constant near zero and affine on the relevant nonzero norm
ranges, then soft maxima. They are smooth psh and converge uniformly;
thus $w_x\in\C$. On an inner neighbourhood of $x$ its curvature is
$\epsilon\DD\psi$, giving $\alpha_x=\epsilon^2D>0$.
The WHOLE bounded measure $\MA(w_x)$ has finite full dual by tangent.
If $u\le0$, $E(u)\ge-C$, (D) implies
\[
-u(x)\le [E^*(\MA(w_x))+C]/\alpha_x<\infty.
\]
We do not infer finite full dual for a normalized Dirac component.
\end{proof}

The classical recognition used here has the following exact source
designations. In GR v2 the smooth CLD-to-classical bridge is the
UNNUMBERED Section 1.2 paragraph; Proposition 4.2 is sheaf, convex/max,
decreasing-NET closure and analytic functoriality; Theorem 6.1 is the
LOCAL maximum principle at relative-interior points; Theorem 6.4 is
the affinoid SHILOV maximum principle. The last is not USC
regularization. Classical psh means the USC all-analytic-curve test
after all analytic complete field extensions, with the $-\infty$
alternative. Finite continuous classical psh functions are locally
uniform-closed: from $\|h_j-h\|\le2^{-j}$ use the decreasing sequence
$h_j+3\cdot2^{-j}$. Minimality recognizes every stage of $\mathscr P$;
decreasing closure recognizes every generated local weight.
The complete immediate proofs of the applied GR units were checked.
Theorem 6.4's printed proof calls its maximum set closed ``since $h$ is
continuous''; USC at the attained supremum already makes it closed,
so no strengthened hypothesis is needed. Wanner 4.7 gives continuous
psh implies Thuillier-subharmonic under its algebraically closed,
complete, nontrivially valued field and smooth proper algebraic curve
standing hypotheses. The equivalence is Corollary 4.8, using 4.5 as
well as 4.7. It is not an arbitrary-surface restriction theorem.

GR Lemma 6.3 and the Abhyankar inequality show that every Shilov point
of every pure two-dimensional affinoid chart has total graded dimension
two. For a classical psh local weight $q$ on a good chart,
\[
q(x)=\inf_{A\ni x\ {\rm affinoid\ neighbourhood}}
\max_{\Gamma_A}q.
\tag{S}
\]
The lower inequality is Theorem 6.4; the reverse follows by USC and
arbitrarily small affinoid neighbourhoods. For $q(x)=-\infty$, use
every finite upper bound. Thus values or order on ALL these Shilov
boundaries determine pointwise weights, including poles.

\section{Independent audit of full generated uniqueness}
We include the curve argument to make clear which identity supplies
pointwise uniqueness; the fixed-probe identity in the next section alone
does not do so. If $\MA(u)=\MA(v)$, (4M) gives $I(a_j,b_j)\to0$
for ANY continuous decreasing presentations. Their upper bounds and
finite lower energies allow fixed shifts and one constant $C$ in (T).
Hence $Q_{\theta_w}(a_j-b_j)\to0$ for each fixed $w\in\C$.

\begin{lemma}\label{disc}
For a complete nontrivially valued $F\supset K$, a full graded-dimension
one point $q$ on $\mathbb G_{m,F}^{\rm an}$, $|z(q)|=r$, lifts after
a FINITE $E/F$ to $\eta_{a,R}$, $a\in E$, $0<R\le r$.
The path $\eta_{a,t}$, $R\le t\le r$, has constant $|z|=r$,
finite logarithmic length $\ell=\log(r/R)$, and ends at $\eta_{0,r}$.
For continuous ambient dpsh restrictions with strong gradients,
\[
|h(q)-h(\eta_{0,r})|^2\le
\ell\int_C\chi\,d'h\wedge d''h
\tag{P}
\]
whenever a nonnegative compact smooth $\chi$ is one on the projected
finite path.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Lift to the completed algebraic closure $C_F$. By CLD 13.8.8(d),
applied only to this Abhyankar line-point presentation, its graded
residue field is finite over the compositum of the old one and
$\widetilde {C_F}$. The latter is algebraic over $\widetilde F$;
completion adds no initial forms. Thus the lift is still full-dimensional.
For its norm let $R=\inf_a|z-a|$, and choose centres with radii
decreasing to $R$. Their discs are nested by the ultrametric inequality.
If the intersection has a centre $a$, factoring polynomials into linear
factors gives the Gauss norm $\eta_{a,R}$. If $R=0$ it is rigid and
has graded dimension zero. If the nested discs have empty intersection,
each $b$ is eventually outside one; the initial form of $z-b$ equals
that of the constant centre minus $b$. All rational-function initials
then belong to the base graded field, as do those of its completion,
again giving dimension zero. Therefore $R>0$ and a Gauss centre exists.
Approximate it by an algebraic $a_0$ within distance $R$ and put
$E=F(a_0)$. The discs agree, so the point over $E$ projects to $q$.
Since $r=\max(|a_0|,R)$, the stated path has the asserted norms and
endpoint.

On the Gauss interval the moment $z-a_0$ has local analytic degree one,
primitive slope one and, by CLD 14.5.2--3, calibration one.
Refining a finite cover of smooth moment charts, unit log norms are
piecewise affine with finitely many breaks on this compact interval.
The positive curve energy restricts to $|H'(\log t)|^2d\log t$;
other branches have nonnegative energy. Cauchy--Schwarz on the finite
interval gives (P) for smooth restrictions. Finite varying-ground-field
integration has factor ONE, by CLD 15.3.1 and 16.1.1:
$\int_{C_E}p^*(\chi d'h\wedge d''h)=\int_C\chi d'h\wedge d''h$.
Uniform/strong approximants pass this inequality to continuous ambient
dpsh restrictions. Their strong convergence on the actual curve is
provided by the positive fibre-current inequality below. No arbitrary
current pullback and no surface infinite scalar extension is used.
\end{proof}

For a nonconstant Laurent polynomial $P(z_2)$, let $\eta$ be its
Gauss image of radius $r_P$. CLD 18.6.1--2, on separated boundaryless
equidimensional spaces, gives the ACTUAL Gauss-fibre current identity
\[
T=\DD\max(0,\log(|P(z_2)|/r_P))=\delta_{P^{-1}(\eta)}.
\tag{F}
\]
Its entire immediate proof is a relative curvature/intersection identity;
the named deeper relative-intersection inputs of CLD 18.3--18.4 remain
conventional foundations. The fibre is a disjoint union of
$\mathbb G_{m,L_\nu}$, with $L_\nu/\HH(\eta)$ finite: the equation
$P(z_2)-T$ has generic transcendental $T$ and is squarefree in
characteristic zero. Viewing such a curve over $\HH(\eta)$ introduces
the positive calibration $\kappa=[L_\nu:\HH(\eta)]$ by 14.4.3.
This is distinct from the normalized field-extension factor one in (P).
On a small box the global bounded cap
$\max(\rho_a,\delta+\epsilon\max(0,\log(|P|/r_P)))-\rho_a$
has $\theta_w=\epsilon T$ on the inner region. For smooth $h$,
positivity and (F) give
\[
Q_{\theta_w}(h)\ge\epsilon\kappa
\int_{\mathbb G_{m,L_\nu}}\chi d'h\wedge d''h
\tag{FT}
\]
for $0\le\chi\le1$ supported in that region. The same inequality
for differences of ambient smooth approximants gives strong convergence
of their actual curve gradients; uniform convergence gives endpoint
values. Thus (FT) and (P) hold for the continuous presentations. They
never assert the restriction of unbounded $u$ to a divisor.

Let $x$ be total full dimension two, with coordinate norms $r_1,r_2$.
Graded tower additivity and the relative Abhyankar inequality imply
that its projection $q_2$ to $z_2$ is full dimension one and that $x$
has relative full dimension one over $\HH(q_2)$. Choose a Laurent
$P(z_2)$ whose initial is transcendental at $q_2$; its image is a
Gauss point. CLD 11.6.5 applies at that full-dimensional image;
equivalently, clearing the Laurent denominator in $P(z_2)-T$, with
transcendental $T$, gives a finite Gauss-fibre algebra. Thus
$L=\HH(q_2)$ is finite over this Gauss field. No global finiteness
over every value of a Laurent polynomial is asserted. The actual fibre
$z_2^{-1}(q_2)=\mathbb G_{m,L}(z_1)$ contains $x$.
Lemma \ref{disc} connects it to the $z_1$-Gauss point $\xi_1$ over
$q_2$ through a finite path with the same norm tuple. The fixed cap for
$P(z_2)$ and (FT),(P),(T) make
$(a_j-b_j)(x)-(a_j-b_j)(\xi_1)\to0$.
The point $\xi_1$ is total full dimension two and projects under $z_1$
to the canonical $K$-Gauss point $\eta_{K,r_1}$.
Its SECOND actual fibre is
$\mathbb G_{m,\HH(\eta_{K,r_1})}(z_2)$. A second finite Gauss-disc
path connects it to the joint Gauss point of radii $r_1,r_2$.
The cap for $z_1$ controls the second endpoint difference. All three
endpoint weights are finite by Proposition \ref{atoms}, so actual
$u-v$ equals its value at that joint Gauss point.
Coordinate-radius finite paths in actual fibres, partitioned into
finitely many injective boxes, connect any two reference Gauss points.
Their fixed caps give one constant on the reference Gauss section and
hence on every full-dimensional point. Formula (S) for ALL affinoid
Shilov boundaries yields $u=v+c$ pointwise, including poles. There is
no analytic map asserted for a varying Shilov section (GR 5.7 warns
against it). Supremum-zero normalization removes the constant.
This is full uniqueness within $\G$, with no existence claim.

\section{Independent audit of the fixed-probe and finite-extension claims}
For finite $F/K$, pullback preserves continuous psh functions and
bounded products. When the finite map is viewed over $K$, its degree
$[F:K]$ is divided by the same calibration factor in CLD 14.4.3 when
one integrates over $F$. CLD 15.3.1 and 16.1.1 therefore give
$p_*B(a_F,b_F)=B(a,b)$, $p_*\MA(a_F)=\MA(a)$ and
$E_F(a_F)=E_K(a)$. Pulling back presentations and passing canonical
limits proves these assertions for $\G$. For finite Galois $F/K$ the
upstairs measures are invariant. Each fibre, described by the finite
etale algebra $\HH(x)\otimes_KF$, is one Galois orbit. Averaging a
continuous test gives an invariant test which descends through the
proper topological quotient; hence invariant Radon measures are
determined by their pushforwards. Equal MA downstairs gives equal MA
upstairs. This does not assert finite-dual preservation for arbitrary
measure lifts or any infinite surface base change.

For a compact smooth $(1,1)$ probe $\alpha$ and FIXED $w\in\C$,
one can dominate $|\alpha\wedge\theta_w|$ by finitely many bounded
MA tests. Here are the analytic details. A finite compact chart cover
tropicalizes $\alpha$ by finitely many analytic units $g_j$.
On a strict rational subdomain its algebra is the completion of the
Laurent coordinate algebra with the rational-domain generators, by the
universal-property rational presentation in Van der Put 2.2.1--2.2.2:
$B=A\langle T_1,\ldots,T_m\rangle/(f_i-f_0T_i)$, where the
$f_0,\ldots,f_m$ have no common zero and $|f_i|\le|f_0|$ on
the domain. Here $f_0$ is a unit in $B$, and polynomials in the
$T_i=f_i/f_0$ with coefficients in $A$ are dense. Laurent truncation
in the surrounding torus polyannulus, followed by an approximation of
$f_0$ below its positive minimum on the compact domain, turns these
finite approximants into Laurent quotients. The bounded division map
is the universal-property proof; no analyticity of a Shilov section is
involved.
Approximate each unit by $A_j/Q_j$ with error below its positive
minimum norm. Ultrametricity gives EXACT equality
$|g_j|=|A_j/Q_j|$ there, hence exact equality of unit-log moments and
differentials. Choose convex smooth $\Phi_\ell$ of the numerator and
denominator logs, with $\Phi''_\ell\ge1$ on their compact norm ranges,
constant near zeros and affine above. The sum $\Psi$ is smooth psh
and bounded on the larger box. A small bounded cap $p_i$ has
$\theta_{p_i}=\epsilon\DD\Psi$ on the inner chart and dominates
both $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$ there, by the elementary coefficient
bound for a finite matrix. A finite nonnegative partition then gives
\[
|\alpha\wedge\theta_w|\le\sum_i c_i B(p_i,w)
\le\sum_i2c_i\MA((p_i+w)/2).
\tag{Pr}
\]
No finiteness of all moment functions on all $X$ is asserted; only the
compact support and its finite charts are used.
By (D), $u\theta_w$ has actual integrable coefficients for $u\in\G$.
After an upper shift its negative is positive order zero; CLD 7.2.9
extends the positive functional. The resulting current is independent
of charts and presentations, which converge coefficientwise in $L^1$
by (Pr). Equal MA, (4M), (T) and Green with compact smooth scalar
tests imply
\[
\DD(u\theta_w-v\theta_w)=0\qquad\text{for EVERY FIXED }w\in\C.
\]
The finite tests and constants may depend on the probe and $w$.
No uniform cap family, unbounded divisor multiplier, divisor limit or
general energy-sublevel uniform integrability follows from this claim.

\section{New quantitative ordered energy-gap estimate}
\begin{theorem}\label{gap}
Suppose $a,b,w\in\C$ are nonpositive, $a\le b$, and each energy
is at least $-C$, $C\ge0$. Put $\delta=E(b)-E(a)$. Then
\[
0\le\int(b-a)\MA(w)\le F_C(\delta),\qquad
F_C(d)=3d+\sqrt{12C\bigl(\tfrac92d+\sqrt{126Cd}\bigr)}.
\tag{EG}
\]
In particular $F_C(d)\to0$ as $d\downarrow0$, without a common
sup-norm lower bound. At a point atom of $\MA(w)$ of size $\alpha$,
$0\le b(x)-a(x)\le F_C(\delta)/\alpha$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $f=b-a\ge0$. By (C),
$\int f\MA(a)\le3\delta$ and
\[
0\le I(a,b)=\int f(\MA(a)-\MA(b))\le3\delta.
\]
With $T=\theta_w+\theta_a$, $k=w-a$, symmetry gives
$\MA(w)-\MA(a)=\DD(kT)$. Green and Cauchy--Schwarz yield
\[
\int f\MA(w)=\int f\MA(a)-Q_T(f,k)
\le3\delta+\sqrt{Q_T(f)Q_T(k)}.
\]
Estimate (T) and $Q_{\theta_a}(f)\le I$ give
$Q_T(f)\le\frac32I+\sqrt{42CI}$.
Also $Q_T(k)=I(a,w)\le\int |a-w|(\MA(a)+\MA(w))\le12C$
by the four bounds in (M). Substituting $I\le3\delta$ proves (EG).
The point estimate uses positivity and the actual atom. If $C=0$, the
same calculation is valid with its zero terms.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{ggap}
The estimate holds for ORDERED actual $u\le v$ in $\G$, with
$\delta=E(v)-E(u)$, after a common upper shift and a correspondingly
fixed energy constant. For each fixed bounded $w$ it bounds
$\int(v-u)\MA(w)$ and every finite full-dimensional point difference.
In particular $u\le v$ and $E(u)=E(v)$ force $u=v$ pointwise.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If $u,v\le B$ and $E(u),E(v)\ge L$, choose any presentations
$A_j\downarrow u$, $B_j\downarrow v$. Replace $B_j$ by
$\max(A_j,B_j)$; it still decreases to $v$ and now dominates $A_j$.
Compact strict domination discards initial terms so both are at most
$B+1$. Subtract $B+1$ from both; energies are at least
$L-2(B+1)$. Independently subtract $\sup_Xw$ from the fixed test.
Choose
\[
C\ge\max\{0,\ 2(B+1)-L,\ -E(w-\sup_Xw)\}.
\]
This single constant works for both presentations. Their energy
differences tend to $E(v)-E(u)$, and their integrals converge by (D).
All full-dimensional endpoint values are finite by Proposition
\ref{atoms}; the point estimate therefore passes to actual limits.
For equal energy all these differences vanish, and (S) proves equality
on all points, including poles. Differences in integrals are assigned
arbitrarily on the common measure-null pole sets.
\end{proof}

\section{New actual closure for arbitrary decreasing nets}
First we give the sequence representation lemma, rather than citing a
supplied note. Suppose $u_k\in\G$ decrease and set
$L=\inf_k E(u_k)>-\infty$. Choose presentations $f_{k,j}$ and enumerate ALL pairs as
$h_1,h_2,\ldots$. Their infimum is the actual $u=\inf_k u_k$.
Set $\epsilon_n=2^{-n}$ and $r_n=\sum_{\ell>n}\epsilon_\ell=2^{-n}$.
Choose $k_n\ge\max(n,k_{n-1})$ so that
$u_{k_n}<h_m+\epsilon_n$ for $m\le n$, by compact strict domination.
For $n>1$, $u_{k_n}\le u_{k_{n-1}}\le v_{n-1}$.
Choose a sufficiently late presentation term $v_n=f_{k_n,j_n}$ so
that it is below all the first $n$ bounds and below
$v_{n-1}+\epsilon_n$. The finitely many strict continuous bounds are
only comparisons, never minima inserted into the psh class.
Then $a_n=v_n+r_n$ decreases, dominates $u$, and eventually lies
below $h_m+\epsilon_n+r_n$ for every $m$. Its exact pointwise limit
is $u$, including poles. Its energies are at least $L$, since
$v_n\ge u_{k_n}$. Thus $u\in\G$. Order gives $E(u)\le L$;
compact strict domination against a presentation of $u$ plus
$\epsilon$ gives the reverse inequality $L\le E(u)$. This proves
countable decreasing closure with $E(u_k)\downarrow E(u)$.

\begin{theorem}\label{net}
Let $(u_i)_{i\in I}$ be ANY directed decreasing net in $\G$,
with $L=\inf_iE(u_i)>-\infty$. Its ACTUAL pointwise infimum
$u=\inf_i u_i$ belongs to the original SEQUENCE-generated class
$\G$, and $E(u_i)\downarrow E(u)=L$. There is a decreasing
sequence of indices selected by energy whose weights have exact
pointwise infimum $u$, although it need not be cofinal in $I$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Restrict to a tail $i\ge i_0$; its infimum and energy infimum agree
with those of the original net by directedness. The USC weight
$u_{i_0}$ is bounded above, so all tail terms have a common finite
upper bound $B$. Recursively choose $i_n\ge i_{n-1}$ with
$E(u_{i_n})\le L+2^{-n}$: find one index with such an energy and
then a directed upper bound, using energy monotonicity.
The sequence lemma gives
$v=\inf_nu_{i_n}\in\G$ and $E(v)=L$.

Fix an arbitrary $i$ and a full-dimensional point $x$. For each $n$
choose $j_n\ge i,i_n$. Then
$u_{j_n}\le u_{i_n}$ and $u_{j_n}\le u_i$;
$0\le E(u_{i_n})-E(u_{j_n})\le2^{-n}$.
All terms are at most $B$ and have energy at least $L$. Corollary
\ref{ggap}, with the fixed atom $w_x$, uses one constant $C_x$
independent of $i,n,j_n$, and gives
\[
0\le u_{i_n}(x)-u_{j_n}(x)
\le F_{C_x}(2^{-n})/\alpha_x\longrightarrow0.
\]
Since $u_{j_n}(x)\le u_i(x)$, taking the limit proves
$v(x)\le u_i(x)$. Conversely $u\le v$, so $u=v$ at ALL
full-dimensional points. This is energy selection, not a hidden
countable cofinality assertion.

The infimum of USC functions is USC. GR Proposition 4.2(4) makes
the local weight $\rho+u$ classical psh by its decreasing-net rule.
The local weight $\rho+v$ is classical psh as generated. All
affinoid Shilov points are full-dimensional; applying (S) to the two
actual local weights shows $u=v$ pointwise, including poles.
Consequently $u\in\G$ and $E(u)=L$ as asserted.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{netcontinuity}
Under Theorem \ref{net}, $\MA(u_i)\to\MA(u)$ weakly against
EVERY continuous analytic-space test. Two or finitely many decreasing
energy-bounded generated nets have canonical mixed-product and moving
moment convergence on a common directed product index. For each positive
Radon $\mu$ of raw mass 2 and $E^*(\mu)<\infty$,
\[
\int|u_i-u|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0.
\]
No support, invariance, metrizability or countable full-support measure
assumption is imposed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every fixed convex combination of the decreasing nets has a finite
lower energy bound by concavity; Theorem \ref{net} supplies its actual
generated limit and energy continuity. At finitely many interpolation
nodes all cubic energy coefficients converge. The first-variation
coefficient identities prove weak convergence against $\C$, all
four moving MA moments and their mixed polarizations. Density of the
span of $\C$ and common mass 2 give every continuous test.

For $L^1(\mu)$, do NOT invoke a general monotone convergence theorem
for arbitrary measurable nets. The actual $u$ has a sequence
presentation $a_m\downarrow u$, which converges in $L^1(\mu)$
by (D). For each $m$ and $\epsilon>0$, compact strict domination
against $a_m+\epsilon$ gives eventually
$u\le u_i<a_m+\epsilon$ everywhere. Hence, outside the common
$\mu$-null pole sets for the individual integrals,
\[
0\le\int(u_i-u)\,d\mu
\le\int(a_m-u)\,d\mu+2\epsilon.
\]
First choose $m$, then $\epsilon$, and take a sufficiently late
index. This proves net $L^1$ convergence. In fact $\{u=-\infty\}$
is a common $\mu$-null set by (D): outside it, $u_i\ge u$ makes every
$u_i$ finite. No assertion about uncountable unions of null sets is needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The theorem also applies to downward filtered families indexed by their
order, and shows that real energy selects an actual sequential infimum
even on this nonmetrizable carrier. It does not say that arbitrary
psh functions with a proposed intrinsic energy belong to $\G$.
Nor can one apply it to the minima or infima of a nonordered family:
those intermediate functions need not be psh or already generated.
The remaining rooftop/envelope step is precisely where such an argument
would need a new input.
Ordinary monotone convergence for arbitrary measurable nets would be
false: on $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure, index by finite subsets $F$
and take $1_{[0,1]\setminus F}$. The net decreases pointwise to zero
while every integral is one. This diagnostic is not an analytic psh
counterexample; the strict-continuous-majorant argument in Corollary
\ref{netcontinuity} supplies the missing condition in the actual theorem.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Geometry and nonalgebraizability}
Tropical translations of $\Lambda$ are exactly $\mathbf Z^2$. Rectangles of
widths less than one give ordinary open injective quotient charts. On bounded
tropical boxes only finitely many deck graphs meet, and each graph is closed.
A finite collection of injective charts covers the compact image of
$x^{-1}([0,1]^2)$. The associated finite atlas map and its product are flat
quasi-finite maps with finite fibres; descent of the closed deck relation
therefore gives a closed diagonal. This does not apply quasi-finite descent
to the infinite-sheeted map $Y\to X$. Thus $X$ is compact Hausdorff,
separated, good, strict, smooth, boundaryless, connected and pure of dimension
two, hence proper. Strict affinoid neighborhoods use rational radii; taking
roots of defining inequalities realizes rational bounds although $|K^*|$
is discrete.

For completeness we reconstruct the obstruction to algebraization.
Let $P_m=\{|s|^m\le |z_i|\le |s|^{-m}\}$.
The unit circle in either coordinate and the adjacent filled disc have trivial
Picard group by Gruson's determinant consequence. Induct on the number of annulus factors in a mixed product of discs,
circles and annuli. To remove one annulus factor, cover the filled disc by
that annulus and its inner disc; their intersection is the inner circle
(rescaled to a unit circle). The intersection and the filled product have
one fewer annulus factors, so their line bundles are trivial by induction.
Glue the given bundle on the annulus product to the trivial bundle on the
inner-disc product, using a frame on the intersection. Tate/Kiehl coherent
gluing produces a bundle on the filled product, whose trivial frame restricts
to the original bundle. The zero-annulus case is Gruson. Thus
$\operatorname{Pic}(P_m)=0$.
A unit $b$ on $P_m$ has affine Gauss log norm: both that norm and its negative
are convex. Consequently its dominant Laurent exponent is constant and
\[
 b=b_\alpha z^\alpha(1+g),\qquad
 \|g\|_{P_j}\le |s|^{m-j}\quad(j<m).
\]
This follows by comparing every other coefficient with the dominant coefficient
at all extreme radii of $P_m$; at $P_j$ every different exponent gains at
least $|s|^{m-j}$. Adjusting frames successively on the exhaustion $P_m$,
removing scalar monomials and multiplying the resulting $1+g$ factors, gives
convergent transition products on every $P_j$. Hence
$\operatorname{Pic}(Y)=0$. The same estimate makes every global unit on $Y$
a scalar monomial.

A line bundle pulled back from $X$ has deck factors $c_1z^{h_1},c_2z^{h_2}$.
Write $h_1=(A,B)$ and $h_2=(C,D)$. Commutation gives
$t^C2^D=3^At^B$, whence $C=B$ by valuation and $A=D=0$ by multiplicative
independence of 2 and 3. Thus $h_1=(0,k),h_2=(k,0)$.
If $k\ne0$, take $\lambda=\lambda_1\lambda_2^{\operatorname{sgn}k}$ and
$h=(k\operatorname{sgn}k,k)$. Then $v(\lambda^h)=2|k|>0$.
An equivariant Laurent series satisfies
\[
 a_{m+jh}=a_m c^j\lambda^{-jm-hj(j+1)/2}.
\]
For $a_m\ne0$ its coefficient valuations go to minus infinity quadratically,
contradicting convergence on every compact polyannulus. There is no nonzero
section. If $k=0$, the two equivariance equations permit at most one exponent;
a nonzero section is a nowhere-zero monomial and all sections are proportional.
For a meromorphic function on $X$, its pole ideal is locally invertible by
regular local factoriality. Its pullback line bundle on $Y$ is trivial; the
numerator and the pole frame become equivariant sections of the same bundle.
The preceding alternatives force their ratio to be constant. Therefore
$\Gamma(X,\mathcal M_X)=K$. If $X$ were the analytification of a proper
algebraic space, smoothness and connectedness would give an integral smooth
algebraic space of dimension two. Its function field, of transcendence degree
two over $K$, embeds in $\Gamma(X,\mathcal M_X)$, a contradiction.
This is a genuine nonalgebraizable carrier with positive raw mass two.

\section{All-stage bounded calculus}
Let $\C$ consist of actual continuous real functions $a$ on $X$ such that
$\rho+a$ belongs locally to the entire minimal continuous CLD psh sheaf.
Set $T_a=\theta+d'd''[a]$. The source products give
\[
 B(a,b)=\theta\wedge T_b+d'd''(aT_b),\qquad
 \MA(a)=B(a,a).
\]
They are positive Radon measures, symmetric, closed, local, and of mass two.
Convex combinations and maxima stay in $\C$: prove these operations for
smooth psh functions by convex smoothing, then use local uniform closure
and minimality separately in the two slots. This proves them at every stage,
not just at the first approximable stage.

\subsection{Green pairing without an unjustified regularization theorem}
For a fixed positive closed $(1,1)$ current $T$, complete compact smooth
$(1,0)$ forms for the pairing $\int\alpha\wedge J\beta\wedge T$ after
quotienting its null space. Smooth compactly supported functions have
$Q_T(f,g)=\int d'f\wedge d''g\wedge T$. Local continuous psh functions
have strong gradients in this Hilbert space, as follows.
Take cutoffs $0\le\chi\le\eta\le1$, with $\eta=1$ near
$\operatorname{supp}\chi$, and a uniform-convergent smooth psh sequence
$f_j$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}\eta$.
For $L_T f=d'd''(fT)$, Stokes gives
\[
 Q_{\chi T}(f_j-f_k,f_j-f_k)
 =\tfrac12\int(f_j-f_k)^2d'd''\chi\wedge T
       -\int\chi(f_j-f_k)L_T(f_j-f_k).
\]
If $\|f_j\|\le B$ there and $\epsilon=\|f_j-f_k\|$, positivity and
$\int\eta L_Tf_j=\int f_jd'd''\eta\wedge T$ bound the right side by
\[
 \tfrac12\epsilon^2\|d'd''\chi\wedge T\|_{\rm TV}
 +2B\epsilon\|\chi\|_\infty\|d'd''\eta\wedge T\|_{\rm TV}.
\]
The gradients are Cauchy. Their limit is unique: against compact smooth
one-forms integration by parts identifies it with the distributional derivative
of the uniform limit. This same estimate works for already constructed strong
gradients. Retain these cutoff and Green identities as part of the constructed class.
They survive its uniform closure: positive $L_Tf_j$ have uniformly bounded
mass on a smaller cutoff, so multiplication by a uniformly converging
continuous coefficient passes to the limit; strong gradients pass the Hilbert
pairings to the limit. Diagonal smooth approximants supply the strong-gradient
definition for that limit. The resulting class of continuous functions with
these identities, strong gradients and positive $L_T$ is a sheaf containing
smooth psh functions and closed under local uniform limits. Minimality puts the entire generated psh sheaf in this class.
Partitions of unity and the bounded multiplier product rule glue the gradients;
a difference of continuous psh functions has the difference gradient.
On compact boundaryless $X$ this gives
\[
 Q_T(f,g)=-\int f\,d'd''(gT)=Q_T(g,f),\qquad
 |Q_T(f,g)|^2\le Q_T(f,f)Q_T(g,g).
\]
Here $f,g$ are continuous dpsh functions, or a smooth test function in one
slot. This argument supplies the Green identities needed below without
assuming a single smooth approximation for every generated function.

Define the cubic energy
\[
 E(a)=\tfrac13\int a\,[\MA(0)+B(a,0)+\MA(a)].
\]
Green, product symmetry and Stokes give $E(0)=0$, $E(a+c)=E(a)+2c$,
\[
 \frac d{dq}E((1-q)a+qb)=\int(b-a)\MA((1-q)a+qb),
\quad
 \frac {d^2}{dq^2}E((1-q)a+qb)
 =-2Q_{T_{(1-q)a+qb}}(b-a,b-a).
\]
Thus $E$ is increasing and concave, and
\[
 E(a)-E(b)=\tfrac13\int(a-b)[\MA(a)+B(a,b)+\MA(b)].             \tag{1}
\]
Locality of products and $\max(a,b-\epsilon)$, whose mass is two, give
bounded comparison on strict inequality sets by letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$.
Equality contacts are not silently assigned either local measure.
\section{Canonical generated energy and actual operators}
Let $\G$ be the set of actual pointwise limits $u=\inf_j u_j$ of decreasing
sequences $u_j\in\C$ with $\inf_jE(u_j)>-\infty$.
These are USC functions, allowed to have poles. No equivalence of functions
modulo measure-zero sets is built into the definition.
If a USC sequence $g_j\downarrow g$ satisfies $g<a$ everywhere for a continuous
$a$ on compact $X$, the increasing open sets $\{g_j<a\}$ cover $X$, hence
some $g_j<a$ globally. Call this strict compact dominance.
For two continuous decreasing presentations of the same $u$, apply it to
$u<a_j+\epsilon$ in both directions. Monotonicity of bounded energy and
$E(a+\epsilon)=E(a)+2\epsilon$ imply that their energy limits agree.
The same proof establishes order monotonicity for generated energy
$E(u)=\lim E(u_j)$. The identically minus-infinity limit is impossible:
strict dominance by each negative constant would force energies to minus
infinity. Convex combinations and finite maxima have continuous decreasing
presentations and finite lower energy bounds by concavity and monotonicity.

On every finite simplex of convex combinations of specified presentations,
$E$ is a polynomial of degree at most three. Evaluating at a finite unisolvent
set of simplex points shows that convergence of energies implies convergence
of every coefficient. The limiting polynomial is intrinsic, because each
point is itself a generated potential and has its canonical energy.
This is a finite-dimensional interpolation argument, not interchange of an
unbounded derivative and a pointwise limit.
For $v\in\C$, set
\[
 P_j(q)=E((1-q)u_j+qv),\qquad R_j(q)=E(qu_j).
\]
Bounded first variation yields
$\int v\MA(u_j)=P_j'(0)+R_j'(1)$; thus these moments converge canonically.

The linear span $\mathcal D$ of $\C$ is uniformly dense in $C(X)$.
Different tropical classes are separated by small smooth periodic perturbations
of $\rho$. Distinct seminorms in the same tropical fibre differ on a Laurent
polynomial $A$. On an injective box $|x_i-a_i|<r<1/2$, put
$\rho_a=|x-a|^2/2$, choose $\delta<r^2/4$, and choose $\epsilon>0$
small enough to glue by zero
\[
 \max\{\rho_a,\delta+\epsilon(\log|A|-b)\}-\rho_a.              \tag{2}
\]
Here $b$ can be chosen so the two specified values are separated. The function
is continuous even at $A=0$, since there it equals zero on a neighborhood;
convex smoothing on $A\ne0$ proves its generated positivity.
The span is a vector lattice. With common positive scale $c$,
\[
 \max\{c(p-q),c(r-s)\}
 =2c\max\{(p+s)/2,(r+q)/2\}-c(q+s).
\]
Here is that lattice density argument explicitly. For any continuous target
$F$ and $\epsilon>0$, point separation and constants give, for each pair
$p,q$, an element agreeing with $F$ at both points. For fixed $p$, finitely
many neighborhoods of $q$ cover $X$ where their elements exceed
$F-\epsilon$. Their maximum exceeds $F-\epsilon$ everywhere and equals
$F(p)$ at $p$, hence is below $F+\epsilon$ near $p$. Finitely many such
neighborhoods of $p$ cover $X$; the minimum of the corresponding maxima
is within $\epsilon$ of $F$ everywhere and belongs to the lattice. Common positive mass two extends the moment convergence
from $\mathcal D$ to all continuous tests. Riesz representation gives an
actual positive Radon measure $\MA(u)$ of mass two, for EVERY continuous
decreasing presentation of $u$. Polarization, equivalently coefficients of
$\MA((u+v)/2)$, gives the positive canonical mixed measure $B(u,v)$.

For a positive Radon measure $\mu$ of mass two define its FULL bounded dual by
\[
 E^*(\mu)=\sup_{a\in\C}\{E(a)-\int a\,d\mu\}.               \tag{3}
\]
No support restriction appears in (3). If $u\le0$ is generated, then
\[
 \int(-u)\,d\mu\le E^*(\mu)-E(u).                          \tag{4}
\]
Indeed apply (3) to $u_j$, then monotone convergence. Constants also show why
mass two is required. Formula (4) proves presentation convergence in
$L^1(\mu)$ and gives $\mu$-null poles whenever the dual is finite.
Bounded tangency gives
$E^*(\MA(a))=E(a)-\int a\MA(a)$ for $a\in\C$.

There is no circular appeal to unbounded self-integrability.
The coefficient $D_u=\lim_j\int u_j\MA(u_j)=\lim R_j'(1)$ is finite.
Taking coefficient limits in bounded tangency gives
$E^*(\MA(u))\le E(u)-D_u<\infty$. Only now may (4) be used for this measure.
For $k\ge j$, (1) gives
\[
 0\le\int(u_j-u_k)\MA(u_k)\le3(E(u_j)-E(u_k)).               \tag{5}
\]
First let $k\to\infty$, using the continuous test $u_j$, coefficient convergence
for the self term, and its newly proved integrability; then let $j\to\infty$.
It follows that
\[
 D_u=\int u\MA(u),\qquad
 E^*(\MA(u))=E(u)-\int u\MA(u).
\]
For $u\le0$, $E(u)\ge-C$, its cubic coefficients give
$\int u\MA(u)\ge3E(u)$ and therefore $E^*(\MA(u))\le2C$.

For clarity, the moving-moment argument has three distinct parts.
For bounded $w$ and generated $u$, the coefficient of $q$ in
$E(pu+qw)$ at $(p,q)=(1,0)$ is $\int w\MA(u)$ by the preceding bounded-test
construction. Next let a continuous decreasing presentation $w_l\downarrow w$
be generated. Energy at every simplex point converges to energy of the
actual convex combination; interpolation gives coefficient convergence.
Finite dual of $\MA(u)$ gives $\int w_l\MA(u)\to\int w\MA(u)$.
Finally make the same interpolation for simultaneous decreasing generated
families $u_j\downarrow u$, $v_j\downarrow v$ whose energies converge.
It yields
\[
 \MA(v_j)\rightharpoonup\MA(v),\quad
 \int u_j\MA(v_j)\to\int u\MA(v),\quad
 \int u\MA(v_j)\to\int u\MA(v).                            \tag{6}
\]
The last assertion uses the fixed-$u$ coefficient argument, not weak convergence
against an unbounded test. Subtracting the last two assertions proves
$\int|u_j-u|\MA(v_j)\to0$. Mixed assertions follow by polarization and
$B(a,b)\le2\MA((a+b)/2)$. For continuous decreasing presentations, energy
convergence is already canonical; for decreasing generated families it will
follow from the countable closure theorem below.

\subsection{Comparison, locality and clamps on actual Borel sets}
The bounded product identities pass to generated strict sets without asserting
that these sets are open. For bounded Lipschitz tests of $u_j-v_j$, first
replace the moving difference by $u-v$ using (6); replace that difference by
fixed continuous approximants $u_l-v_l$ using the fixed-slot moment convergence;
then use weak convergence at fixed $l$ and let $l\to\infty$.
Lipschitz ramps converge to strict-set indicators at levels carrying no mass.
Only countably many levels are bad for the finitely many measures involved,
so approach zero through good levels. This proves
\[
 \MA(v)\{u<v\}\le\MA(u)\{u<v\},\qquad
 \mathbf1_{\{u>v\}}\MA(\max(u,v))
   =\mathbf1_{\{u>v\}}\MA(u).                              \tag{7}
\]
The same argument and polarization give mixed maximum locality.
Borel restrictions of a finite Radon measure on compact Hausdorff $X$ are
Radon; continuous-test equality therefore identifies the restrictions.
For $u\le0$, put $u^A=\max(u,-A)$. This is generated, even if discontinuous.
Then $\mathbf1_{\{u>-A\}}\MA(u^A)=\mathbf1_{\{u>-A\}}\MA(u)$.
If $E(u)\ge-C$, (4) and $E^*(\MA(u^A))\le2C$ give discarded mass
at most $3C/A$. The entire contact set $u=-A$ is excluded.
Mixed clamp restrictions have discarded mass at most
$2(2C_u+C_v)/A+2(C_u+2C_v)/B$ on the complement of
$\{u>-A,v>-B\}$. These are actual generated products; they do not identify
bounded discontinuous clamps with the preexisting continuous CLD operator.

\section{Constrained countable decreasing closure}
\begin{theorem}
If $u_k\in\G$ decreases pointwise and $L=\inf_kE(u_k)>-\infty$, its actual
pointwise infimum $u$ belongs to $\G$, and $E(u_k)\downarrow E(u)$.
It has a single continuous decreasing presentation, also at its poles.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose presentations $f_{k,j}\in\C$ with $f_{k,j}\downarrow u_k$.
Enumerate ALL inner terms as $h_1,h_2,\ldots$; their pointwise infimum is $u$.
Let $\epsilon_n=2^{-n}$ and $r_n=\sum_{\ell>n}\epsilon_\ell=2^{-n}$.
Choose $k_n\ge\max(n,k_{n-1})$ such that
$u_{k_n}<h_m+\epsilon_n$ globally for every $m\le n$.
Each bound follows from strict compact dominance for the decreasing USC outer
sequence, because $u\le h_m<h_m+\epsilon_n$. Taking finitely many bounds
is legitimate. Choose an inner term $v_n=f_{k_n,j_n}$ satisfying these bounds
and, for $n>1$, $v_n<v_{n-1}+\epsilon_n$ globally. Indeed
$u_{k_n}\le u_{k_{n-1}}\le v_{n-1}$, so strict compact dominance applies
to this additional continuous upper bound as well.
Then $a_n=v_n+r_n\in\C$ is decreasing, since
$\epsilon_n+r_n=r_{n-1}$. It dominates $u$ and, for fixed $m$, is eventually
below $h_m+\epsilon_n+r_n$. Consequently $\inf_na_n=\inf_mh_m=u$,
including where that infimum is minus infinity. Monotonicity gives
$E(a_n)\ge E(u_{k_n})\ge L$, so $u\in\G$.
For any continuous presentation $b_j\downarrow u$ and any $\epsilon>0$,
strict compact dominance gives $u_k<b_j+\epsilon$ globally for late $k$.
Hence $\lim_kE(u_k)\le E(b_j)+2\epsilon$; let $j\to\infty$ and
$\epsilon\downarrow0$. The reverse inequality is order monotonicity.
\end{proof}
This is not a net, cofinality, or energy-sublevel compactness theorem.
It now justifies (6) for every energy-bounded decreasing generated family.
A countable directed family has a decreasing cofinal choice, with the same
pointwise infimum. If $u_i\le0$, $\sum_i\lambda_i\le1$, and
$\sum_i\lambda_i|E(u_i)|<\infty$, the finite sums (with the remaining
coefficient assigned to zero) decrease and have energies bounded below by
concavity. The theorem gives their actual generated sum and energy continuity.
No convergence of a nonordered variational family is deduced.
\section{All-test control and bounded pointwise uniqueness}
For $a,b,w\in\C$ set $f=a-b$, $g=(a+b)/2$, $h=w-g$ and
\[
 I(a,b)=\int(a-b)[\MA(b)-\MA(a)].
\]
The actual bounded Green calculus gives
\[
 I=Q_{T_a}(f,f)+Q_{T_b}(f,f)\ge0,
\qquad
 Q_{T_w}(f,f)-Q_{T_g}(f,f)
   =Q_{T_a}(f,h)-Q_{T_b}(f,h).                              \tag{8}
\]
The second identity is the symmetric transgression
$-\int f\,d'd''f\wedge d'd''h$, not pullback of a current.
Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 Q_{T_w}(f,f)\le I/2+
 \sqrt{I\,[Q_{T_a}(h,h)+Q_{T_b}(h,h)]}.                     \tag{9}
\]
Shift $a,b,w$ separately to be nonpositive and choose a common $C$ with
$E(a),E(b),E(w)\ge-C$. Constants do not affect (8).
By (4), $\int(-p)\MA(q)\le3C$ for these functions, and mixed moments are
at most $6C$. Since $|h|\le-w+(-a-b)/2$, its absolute MA moments are
at most $6C$ and its mixed moments at most $12C$.
Expanding $Q_{T_a}(h,h)=-\int h\,d'd''h\wedge T_a$ bounds it by
$12C+3C+6C=21C$; the same holds for $b$. Thus
\[
 Q_{T_w}(a-b,a-b)\le I(a,b)/2+\sqrt{42C I(a,b)}.             \tag{10}
\]
For $u,v\in\G$ with equal actual MA measures, take continuous presentations
$u_j,v_j$. Moving and fixed moments (6) give $I(u_j,v_j)\to0$, hence
$Q_{T_w}(u_j-v_j,u_j-v_j)\to0$ for EVERY fixed $w\in\C$.
Degeneracy of $\theta$ on residue bidiscs prevents replacing this by a
constancy assertion from $Q_\theta$ alone.

\subsection{Divisor identity for a bounded continuous defect}
If $a,b\in\C$ have equal MA, (10) and Green against any compact smooth
scalar test give $d'd''((a-b)T_w)=0$ for every $w\in\C$.
Write $d=a-b$. On a smaller injective torus box and for a Laurent polynomial
$A$, let $\psi_N=\chi(\log|A|+N)$, where $\chi$ is smooth convex
nondecreasing, zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and $\chi(q)=q-c$ for $q\ge1$.
It is globally smooth, including at zeros of $A$.
Choose a convex-cap weight
\[
 w_N=\max\{\rho_a,\delta+\epsilon_N\psi_N\}-\rho_a
\]
which vanishes on a tropical boundary collar. In the inner box
$\rho_a<\delta/2$ it has $T_{w_N}=\epsilon_Nd'd''\psi_N$.
Therefore $d'd''(d\,d'd''\psi_N)=0$ there.
On the support of a compact smooth top-degree test, zeros of $A$ are absent
from its full-dimensional support. Its compact support has $|A|$ bounded
away from zero, so $\psi_N-N$ eventually equals $\log|A|-c$ there.
Poincare--Lelong gives positive-current convergence
$d'd''\psi_N\to\delta_{\operatorname{div}A}$ locally.
CLD 8.5.1 permits the continuous multiplier $d$ in this limit; consequently
\[
 d'd''(d\,\delta_{\operatorname{div}A})=0.                  \tag{11}
\]
This uses continuity and boundedness of $d$ in an essential way.

For a local principal holomorphic function $F$, work on a strict rational
domain $V$ in a compact polyannulus. Present
$\mathcal O(V)=A\langle r_i^{-1}T_i\rangle/(g_0T_i-g_i)$;
$g_0$ is a unit on $V$ with positive minimum norm.
Truncate a representative Tate series and approximate its finitely many
coefficients and $g_i$ by Laurent polynomials. Approximate $g_0$ by $q$
with error below its minimum norm. Substituting $T_i=g_i/g_0$ and choosing
errors small enough for the finite truncated expression yields
$F_n=A_n/Q_n\to F$ uniformly on $V$, with Laurent numerators and unit
Laurent denominators. The denominators stay controlled; none acquires a
zero on $V$. On each compact full-dimensional smooth test support avoiding
$F=0$, the equality $|F_n|=|F|$ is eventually exact. Hence their log currents
converge there. Poincare--Lelong identifies the positive divisor currents;
unit denominators contribute no divisor. Apply (11) and the continuous
multiplier theorem to conclude (11) for EVERY local principal holomorphic
divisor. This does not prove integrability of an unbounded defect on divisors.

\subsection{Coordinate curves, finite Galois averaging, and Gauss rays}
We give the full bounded uniqueness route, needing only coordinate curves.
Let $P\in K[z_1]$ be irreducible with nonzero constant term and
$L=K[z_1]/(P)$. Characteristic zero makes $P$ separable. The principal
curve $C_P=\{P(z_1)=0\}\subset Y$ is reduced smooth, is $\mathbf G_{m,L}$
viewed over $K$, and its closed immersion $j$ is proper with divisor
multiplicity one. Pullback of a continuous generated psh function belongs to
the corresponding curve sheaf: this holds for smooth generators, is local,
and survives uniform limits, so minimality applies at every stage.
Thus $d|_{C_P}$ is continuous dpsh and its Laplacian is a signed Radon
measure. Projection and push-differentiation turn (11) into
\[
 j_*d'd''[d|_{C_P}]=0.
\]
A closed embedding has injective pushforward on scalar signed Radon measures:
a measure is determined on its closed image, and compact continuous tests
extend locally to the ambient locally compact Hausdorff space.
Its curve Laplacian is therefore zero. Its $K$ calibration is $[L:K]$
times its $L$ calibration, so it is also zero over $L$.

Here is the field-change step independently of any pullback of currents.
For a finite Galois extension $E/L$, let $\pi:\mathbf G_{m,E}^{\rm an}
\to\mathbf G_{m,L}^{\rm an}$. Pull back the continuous dpsh function $h$,
and form its Laplacian upstairs. This is a signed Radon measure $\nu$,
not a formal pullback of the downstairs current. It is Galois invariant by
naturality of function pullback and differentiation. Projection and normalized
fundamental pushforward give $\pi_*\nu=d'd''[h]=0$.
For any analytic point $x$, $\mathcal H(x)\otimes_LE$ is a finite etale
algebra, a product of complete fields. The Galois group acts transitively
on the factors, since its invariants are $\mathcal H(x)$ and a proper union
of orbits would give a nontrivial invariant idempotent. Unique extension of
the complete valuation gives exactly one point per factor. Thus every fibre
is a single Galois orbit. The finite proper map is the topological quotient.
Average a compact continuous test over the finite group; the average descends
to a compact continuous test downstairs. Invariance of $\nu$ and
$\pi_*\nu=0$ imply every test integral is zero. Hence $\nu=0$.
The push has factor one over varying ground fields; viewing the source over
$L$ instead would have the factor $[E:L]$. No infinite extension is used.

If $h$ is bounded continuous dpsh on $\mathbf G_{m,E}^{\rm an}$ and
$d'd''[h]=0$, set $H_0(q)=h(\eta_{0,e^{-q}})$ on $\mathbf R$.
Torus integration with degree-one lattice gives, for every compact smooth
$\varphi$, $\int H_0(q)\varphi''(q)dq=0$.
A continuous distribution with zero second derivative is affine; boundedness
makes it constant. For $a\in E^*$ use the annulus coordinate $z-a$ on
$0<r<|a|$. The same calibration proves
$H_a(q)=h(\eta_{a,e^{-q}})$ is affine on the corresponding halfline,
and boundedness again makes it constant. As $r\downarrow0$ these points
converge to $a$; as $r\uparrow|a|$ they converge to
$\eta_{a,|a|}=\eta_{0,|a|}$. Continuity identifies $h(a)$ with the same
constant on the central Gauss ray.
Every closed rigid point over $L$ becomes rational over a finite Galois normal
closure of its finite residue extension, so the preceding argument proves
its value equals this constant downstairs. Closed rigid points are dense:
every ordinary open set contains a strict rational neighborhood in a strict
affinoid domain, and a nonempty such algebra has a maximal ideal with finite
residue field by the strict Tate Nullstellensatz. Continuity therefore makes
$h$ constant on the whole curve.

At a rigid point $(a,b)$ of $Y$, the vertical curve given by the minimal
polynomial of $a$ connects its value to the rigid point $(a,1)$.
The horizontal curve $z_2=1$, by the same argument, has constant defect.
All rigid values of $d$ on $Y$ are equal; strict-affinoid density and continuity
make $d$ constant on $Y$ and therefore on $X$.
We have proved bounded CONTINUOUS uniqueness modulo constants on the actual
specified $X$. This corrects the old current400 residual phrase saying that
bounded uniqueness was still open. It proves no bounded-discontinuous or
unbounded generated uniqueness theorem.

\section{Classical recognition and the precise Shilov gate}
The applied GR v2 source is the paragraph in Section 1.2 that smooth CLD psh
functions are classically psh, using Wanner and smooth pullback; it is not a
formal theorem numbered 1.2. Wanner's actual continuous equivalence is
Corollary 4.8, combining Theorems 4.5 and 4.7, on open subsets of a smooth
proper algebraic curve over an algebraically closed complete nontrivially
valued field. GR uses this on the tested curves; it is not directly invoked
for a nonalgebraizable surface. GR 4.2 gives the affinoid maximum principle;
6.1 supplies decreasing closure (with the extended minus-infinity convention);
6.4 supplies upper semicontinuous regularization and its Hartogs upper control,
under its stated boundedness hypotheses. Their immediate proofs were read.
A uniform sequence can be replaced by a decreasing sequence by taking a
subsequence with errors $2^{-j}$ and adding $3\cdot2^{-j}$.
Minimality and decreasing closure consequently give classical recognition of
ALL continuous generated weights and of their actual decreasing limits,
on every curve test and every field extension in that definition.
This is classical recognition, not construction of extended mixed products
from one positive Hessian.

For a USC classically psh local weight $q$ and an actual affinoid neighborhood
basis $A$ at a point $x$, the maximum principle and USC give
\[
 q(x)=\inf_{A\ni x}\max_{\xi\in\Gamma_A}q(\xi).             \tag{12}
\]
One inequality is the maximum principle; for the other shrink $A$ into
$\{q<q(x)+\epsilon\}$. If $q(x)=-\infty$, shrink into $\{q<-N\}$ for
arbitrary $N$. Thus values on ALL the varying Shilov boundaries determine
actual USC weights, including poles. A dense set alone does not do this.
The finite-boundary cover argument, with small oscillation of a continuous
obstacle on each affinoid, gives Hartogs UPPER control. It gives neither
lower tails nor actual representatives of nonordered limiting families.
\section{New progress: finite scalar extension for the generated operator}
\begin{theorem}\label{finite}
Let $F/K$ be finite, $\pi:X_F\to X$, and use the respective-ground-field
CLD calibrations on the two spaces. The same torus quotient and curvature
construction over $F$ has classes $\C_F,\G_F$ and raw mass two.
For $u,v\in\G$,
\[
 u\circ\pi\in\G_F,\quad E_F(u\circ\pi)=E_K(u),\quad
 \pi_*B_F(u\circ\pi,v\circ\pi)=B_K(u,v).                   \tag{13}
\]
In particular (13) holds for MA, for every continuous decreasing presentation,
and for the finite mixed moments of pulled-back generated functions.
If $F/K$ is Galois and $\MA_K(u)=\MA_K(v)$, then
$\MA_F(u\circ\pi)=\MA_F(v\circ\pi)$ as actual measures upstairs.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The quotient atlas and $\rho$ are defined by the same Laurent formulas over
$F$. The compact fundamental polyannulus and finite-atlas construction
commute with finite scalar extension, giving $X_F=Y_F/\Lambda$ and a proper
finite scalar map. The Green argument, bounded products, density of bounded
caps, polynomial interpolation and countable closure above use these local
torus charts and compactness, so reconstruct the same actual classes and
operators over $F$. They do not require nonalgebraizability over $F$.
Pullback preserves smooth psh generators and local uniform convergence;
minimality proves $\pi^*\C\subset\C_F$ at all stages.

For bounded $a,b$, the proper projection formula for continuous dpsh products
applies to these functions, not to an arbitrary current pullback.
One may view $X_F$ over $K$: its fundamental current pushes to
$[F:K]\delta_X$. Calibration of ALL its integrals of the pulled-back forms
and their generated products over $K$ is $[F:K]$ times calibration over $F$,
by 14.4.3. Divide the same-field projection equality by this nonzero degree.
It gives
$\pi_*B_F(a\pi,b\pi)=B_K(a,b)$ and also the coefficient-weighted equality
for every continuous function pulled back from $X$.
The three terms of the cubic energy therefore give
$E_F(a\pi)=E_K(a)$. This derivation retains the degree in the intermediate
same-field expression rather than confusing it with the varying-field rule.

A continuous decreasing presentation $u_j$ pulls back pointwise to $u\pi$,
with the same energies. Thus it is a presentation in $\G_F$ and its canonical
energy is the same. For every continuous test downstairs, proper pushforward
and weak convergence of the bounded mixed products give (13).
Finiteness and equality of moments follow either from the generated moment
construction or from the pushforward identity and ordinary integration of
the actual Borel functions; poles have zero mixed mass by (4) and polarization.

For Galois $F/K$, the products of pulled-back bounded functions are invariant
under the finite semilinear Galois action. Locally this action preserves the
absolute value, the coordinate moment functions, their calibration and the
smooth calculus. It preserves smooth generators and their uniform closure;
naturality of continuous products then gives invariance. Weak convergence
preserves it for generated MA and mixed measures.
The fibre argument using $\mathcal H(x)\otimes_KF$ given above applies to
ANY analytic point of $X$. Hence fibres are single Galois orbits and $\pi$
is a proper quotient map. If two invariant measures have the same pushforward,
their invariant signed difference integrates a test just as it integrates its
finite Galois average. That average descends to a continuous test downstairs.
Their difference is zero. Applying (13) proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}
No assertion is made that the full dual (3) of an arbitrary measure pulls
back unchanged: $\C_F$ includes tests that need not descend.
No infinite field extension, pullback of arbitrary currents, or general
upstairs equation theory is used.

\section{New progress: domination of probes and an unbounded defect current}
\begin{lemma}\label{dom}
Fix $w\in\C$. For every compactly supported smooth symmetric $(1,1)$ form
$\alpha$ on $X$, the signed coefficient measure
$\mu_{\alpha,w}=\alpha\wedge T_w$ satisfies
\[
 |\mu_{\alpha,w}|\le\sum_{i=1}^m c_i B(p_i,w)
 \le\sum_{i=1}^m2c_i\MA((p_i+w)/2)                         \tag{14}
\]
for finitely many $p_i\in\C$ and finite $c_i>0$.
Every analytic moment used by $\alpha$ is allowed; the lemma is not confined
to the reference tropicalization. The antisymmetric part of a general probe
pairs to zero with the symmetric $T_w$, by the $J$ symmetry of top-degree
integration, so symmetric probes suffice to define the entire coefficient
current.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Cover the support by finitely many small injective tropical boxes. Within each,
choose an ordinary smaller neighborhood compactly contained in a strict
rational domain of a compact polyannulus, on which a finite list of analytic
units $g_1,\ldots,g_m$ presents the smooth form.
Smooth nonnegative cutoffs subordinate to these neighborhoods decompose
$\alpha$ into finitely many compactly supported pieces $\alpha_i$.
The form has symmetric coefficient matrix in the $d'\log|g_j|,
 d''\log|g_j|$ coordinates; its coefficients are bounded on a compact
neighborhood of the support.

Use the rational-domain approximation already proved, now on each analytic
unit $g_j$. Its minimum norm on that compact domain is positive.
Choose a Laurent rational approximant $A_j/Q_j$ with unit denominator and
uniform error strictly smaller than that minimum. The ultrametric inequality
gives EXACTLY $|g_j|=|A_j/Q_j|$ everywhere on the domain; in particular
$A_j$ is a unit there too. On its interior,
\[
 \log|g_j|=\log|A_j|-\log|Q_j|.
\]
This is equality of smooth moment functions, so it preserves their first
forms and all the coefficient representations of $\alpha_i$.
Let $H_\ell$ be the finite list of all these Laurent numerators and denominators.
Their log norms lie in finite intervals on a compact neighborhood of
$\operatorname{supp}\alpha_i$.
Choose smooth convex nondecreasing scalar functions $\Phi_\ell$ which vanish
below a lower cutoff, have $\Phi_\ell''\ge1$ on those intervals, and are
affine above an upper cutoff. Put
$\Psi=\sum_\ell\Phi_\ell(\log|H_\ell|)$.
It is globally smooth and psh on the injective tropical box: near a zero of
an $H_\ell$ its summand is locally constant zero, and away from zeros the
log norm is smooth pluriharmonic. It is nonnegative and bounded above on
the whole box, because Laurent polynomial norms are uniformly bounded above
on its compact tropical closure. On the chosen compact neighborhood,
\[
 d'd''\Psi\ \ge\ \sum_\ell
 d'\log|H_\ell|\wedge d''\log|H_\ell|.                     \tag{15}
\]
The elementary symmetric-matrix inequality bounds both $\alpha_i$ and
$-\alpha_i$ by a finite multiple of the right side of (15): differences of
two moment gradients cost at most twice the sum of their squares, and the
bounded coefficient matrix costs its finite operator norm. In dimension two,
all the positivity conventions agree for $(1,1)$ forms; no higher-degree
cone interior is being asserted.

Write $\rho_a=|x-a|^2/2$ in this box. Shrink the compact support neighborhood
so $\rho_a<\delta/2$, and choose $\delta$ strictly below the minimum of
$\rho_a$ on a tropical boundary collar. Choose $\epsilon>0$ so small that
$\delta+\epsilon\sup\Psi<\rho_a$ on that collar. Then
\[
 p_i=\max\{\rho_a,\delta+\epsilon\Psi\}-\rho_a,
\]
extended by zero, is in $\C$ and satisfies
$T_{p_i}=\epsilon d'd''\Psi$ near the support. Both
$c_iT_{p_i}+\alpha_i$ and $c_iT_{p_i}-\alpha_i$ are positive there for
large enough finite $c_i$; outside the support they are positive because
$T_{p_i}$ is positive. Near the support $T_{p_i}=\epsilon d'd''\Psi$ is SMOOTH,
so wedging either positive smooth form with the positive $T_w$ preserves
positivity. Away from the support the desired measure is the positive
continuous product $B(p_i,w)$. Locality therefore gives signed-measure inequalities
$-c_iB(p_i,w)\le\alpha_i\wedge T_w\le c_iB(p_i,w)$.
Total variation is bounded by this positive dominating measure. Sum the
pieces and use
$B(p_i,w)\le2\MA((p_i+w)/2)$, which follows by expanding the positive
square. This proves (14).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{unbounded}
For EVERY $u\in\G$ and fixed $w\in\C$, the coefficient product $uT_w$
is a well-defined order-zero current obtained by integrating the actual
function $u$ against each coefficient measure. Every continuous decreasing
presentation $u_j\downarrow u$ converges to it in coefficient $L^1$ and
weakly as currents. If $u,v\in\G$ and $\MA(u)=\MA(v)$, then
\[
 d'd''(uT_w-vT_w)=0\qquad\hbox{for EVERY fixed }w\in\C.    \tag{16}
\]
This is an unbounded current identity, not pointwise uniqueness.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every MA measure on the right of (14) has finite FULL dual by the proved
bounded tangency, so (4), after shifting $u$ by a constant, proves
$u\in L^1(|\mu_{\alpha,w}|)$ and
$\int|u_j-u|d|\mu_{\alpha,w}|\to0$. Its poles are null for all those
coefficient measures. Define the product separately for each actual function;
there is no subtraction of two infinite point values.
Since $u$ has a finite upper bound $b$, the functional
$\alpha\mapsto\int(b-u)\alpha\wedge T_w$ is finite, linear, and positive
on positive compact smooth $(1,1)$ forms. CLD 7.2.9 makes it order zero.
Subtracting it from $bT_w$ constructs $uT_w$. The coefficient convergence
above proves current convergence of $u_jT_w$ to this product.

Choose continuous decreasing presentations $u_j,v_j$ with uniform lower
energy bounds and put $f_j=u_j-v_j$.
Equations (6) and (10) give $Q_{T_w}(f_j,f_j)\to0$.
For every compact smooth scalar test $\varphi$, Green and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 |\langle d'd''(f_jT_w),\varphi\rangle|
 =|Q_{T_w}(f_j,\varphi)|
 \le Q_{T_w}(f_j,f_j)^{1/2}Q_{T_w}(\varphi,\varphi)^{1/2}
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
The fixed smooth test has finite second factor. Differentiation commutes with
weak current convergence. Passing to the coefficient-current limit proves
(16). This proof covers ALL local smooth moment probes through Lemma
\ref{dom}, not just those depending on $x_1,x_2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A precise limit that remains unjustified}
The caps in the bounded divisor proof vary with $N$. The constants $c_i$ in
(14), and the dual energies of their dominating measures, depend on the cap
and need not be bounded in that limit. Thus (16) cannot currently be passed
to $d'd''((u-v)\delta_D)=0$ for a divisor $D$. Neither existence of a divisor
restriction nor uniform integrability for this limit has been proved.
The continuous multiplier theorem 8.5.1 does not apply to $u-v$ at its poles.
This identifies a specific remaining obstacle in the extension of bounded
coordinate-curve uniqueness to the actual unbounded domain.

There is a useful conditional point estimate which does not cross that obstacle.
If a bounded test $w$ has $\MA(w)\{\xi\}=c>0$, then for $u\le0$,
$E(u)\ge-C$, (4) gives
\[
 -u(\xi)\le\frac{E^*(\MA(w))+C}{c}<\infty.                \tag{17}
\]
No real positive atom at EVERY full-dimensional Abhyankar/Shilov point has
been constructed here. Nor does the fact that $c\delta_\xi$ is a component
of one finite-dual measure imply that $2\delta_\xi$ itself has finite full
dual. Formula (17) is consequently a conditional estimate, not a claimed
point-capacity theorem or separated energy compactness.

The ORIGINAL target remains: construct the finite-energy operator and its
existence-and-uniqueness theory on genuinely nonalgebraizable analytic spaces,

remaining gates are all still imposed:
\begin{enumerate}

for nonordered variational limits. Countable downward closure does not supply it.
\item Separated normalized energy-sublevel compactness in a specified topology,

No full original P16.7 solution or analytic counterexample is claimed.
