\begin{abstract}
For the specified compact analytic torus quotient, two bounded
continuous potentials in the entire minimal continuous CLD psh sheaf
with the same actual Monge--Ampere measure differ by a constant.
We include the bounded Green argument and divisor testing, then prove
a bounded harmonic Liouville lemma for the analytic multiplicative
group over finite extensions of the actual base field. Finite Galois
descent of signed Radon Laplacians, calibrated Gauss-ray integration,
and density of closed rigid points suffice. Coordinate algebraic
curves then connect the values of the difference; no recognition by
all analytic curves after arbitrary scalar extensions is assumed.
All claims are working claims pending independent review. The result
does not settle unbounded finite-energy uniqueness, finite-energy
compactness, obstacle orthogonality, or general equation existence.
\end{abstract}

\section{Carrier, domain, and exact foundations}
Put $K=\mathbb C((s))$, $|s|=e^{-1/8}$, and let
\[
 X=((\mathbb G_m)^2)^{\mathrm{an}}/
 \langle(s^8,2),(3,s^8)\rangle,
 \qquad x_i=-\log|z_i|,
 \quad \rho=\tfrac12|x|^2,
 \quad\theta=\DD\rho.
\]
We retain the compact, connected, smooth, good, boundaryless analytic
quotient and its ordinary injective torus-chart atlas as geometric
foundations. Tropical translation by the periods is $\mathbb Z^2$;
rectangles of coordinate width less than one give injective charts.
The local reference potentials differ by affine functions of unit
logarithms, so their Hessians glue. Quotient existence, separatedness,
properness and nonalgebraization are separate geometric statements;
the present theorem does not reestablish their entire proof trees.

Let $\mathscr P$ be the minimal sheaf of finite continuous functions
containing ordinary smooth CLD psh functions and closed under locally
uniform limits. Let
\[
 \mathcal C=\{u\in C(X,\mathbb R):\rho+u\in\mathscr P
                         \text{ on every chart}\}.
\]
Here every continuous-sheaf stage is retained. Convex combinations and
finite maxima preserve this class: prove the assertions for smooth
weights by convexity and smooth convex soft maxima, then use minimality
and uniform closure successively in the two slots.

The immediately applied CLD v2 foundations are Definition8.1.7 and
Lemma8.1.8; Lemmas8.5.1,8.5.3,8.5.5; the symmetric recursive continuous
products in8.7.1,8.7.2,8.7.4; multilinear continuous dpsh calculus and
smooth null changes in8.8.4--5; scalar Radon recognition and
smooth-coefficient measures in7.2.8,7.2.11--12; compact-support
Green/Stokes in5.11.1; calibrated integration15.7.1; and
Poincare--Lelong16.7.3~\cite{CLD}.
They give positive closed products, local uniform continuity, and the
following multiplier rule: if positive currents $T_j$ converge weakly
to $T$ and continuous coefficients converge locally uniformly, their
products converge weakly. We use only scalar and surface $(1,1)$
positivity; no higher-degree strong-cone order unit is assumed.
Smooth cutoffs and the underlying calibrated integration are ordinary
published foundations. The whole immediate applied source units were
read; deeper recursive proofs are not all newly audited.

We also use the defining Tate-algebra presentation of a rational domain
and the density of finite polynomials in a completed Tate algebra;
the latter follows directly by truncating its convergent series.
The ordinary presentation and its universal-property argument are
Van der Put2.1--2.2~\cite{VdP}; the strict presentation is also stated
in Papikian3.4--3.5~\cite{Pap}.
This includes generalized polyannulus radii. Rational domains form a
compact neighborhood basis inside a good affinoid torus chart.
These are ordinary affinoid foundations, not a claimed approximation
by polynomials on an arbitrary open set without shrinking.

\section{Bounded Green calculus at all continuous stages}
Fix a positive closed $(1,1)$ current $T$. Complete compact smooth
$(1,0)$ forms modulo the null space of the positive pairing
$\int a\wedge Jb\wedge T$. With a nonnegative compact smooth cutoff
$\chi$, write the local gradient pairing as $Q_{T,\chi}$.
Let $\mathscr H_T$ consist of continuous functions locally approximable
uniformly by smooth functions whose gradients converge strongly in
these cutoff seminorms.

Gradients are unique: if smooth $f_j\to0$ uniformly and their gradients
converge strongly to $a$, then, for each compact smooth form $b$,
closedness of $T$ gives
\[
 \int d'f_j\wedge Jb\wedge T
 =-\int f_jd'(Jb)\wedge T\longrightarrow0.
\]
The right side pairs $f_j$ with a finite signed measure. Smooth forms
are dense in the completion, so $a=0$. Smaller patches and cutoffs
give the same local assertion. Smooth partitions patch approximants:
the gradient of $\sum\chi_i f_{i,j}$ splits into
$\sum\chi_i d'f_{i,j}+\sum f_{i,j}d'\chi_i$, with both sums strongly
convergent. Bounded continuous multiplication of forms follows by
scalar smooth approximation and the norm bound. Products and cutoffs
of functions in $\mathscr H_T$ therefore have the usual gradient rule.

If $f\in\mathscr H_T$ and $L_Tf=\DD(fT)$ is signed Radon, smooth
approximation first in $f$, then uniformly and strongly in a compactly
supported $g\in\mathscr H_T$, proves
\[
 \int gL_Tf=-Q_T(f,g).
\]
In particular the product rule yields
\[
 Q_{T,\chi}(w,w)
 =\tfrac12\int w^2\DD\chi\wedge T-\int\chi w L_Tw.
\]
The sheaf of $f\in\mathscr H_T$ with $L_Tf\ge0$ contains smooth psh
functions and is uniformly closed. Indeed choose nested cutoffs
$\chi,\eta$, with $\eta=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, and a common
bound $|f_j|\le B$ on the whole support of $\eta$. For
$\epsilon=\|f_j-f_k\|$ there, positivity and integration by parts give
\[
 0\le Q_{T,\chi}(f_j-f_k,f_j-f_k)
 \le\tfrac{\epsilon^2}{2}\|\DD\chi\wedge T\|_{TV}
 +2B\epsilon\|\chi\|_\infty\|\DD\eta\wedge T\|_{TV}.
\]
To obtain smooth approximants to the limit on a smaller patch, choose
an approximant to each $f_j$ with uniform and gradient error at most
$1/j$ for a cutoff equal to one on that patch. The displayed estimate
proves strong convergence. Positivity survives distributional limits.
Minimality now puts all of $\mathscr P$ in this sheaf. Its vector span
contains continuous dpsh functions. Finite patching on compact $X$
proves the global formula
\[
 \int f\DD(gT)=\int g\DD(fT)=-Q_T(f,g),
 \qquad Q_T(f,f)\ge0,
\]
and Cauchy--Schwarz for continuous dpsh functions. This argument uses
positive Laplacians and signed measures, not arbitrary continuous
multiplier closedness.

For $u\in\mathcal C$ write $\theta_u=\theta+\DD u$ and
$B(u,v)=\theta_u\wedge\theta_v$ for the actual recursive local
products, glued through the smooth null potential changes.
Set $\MA(u)=B(u,u)$. Every mixed measure has the same finite mass
$M=\int\theta^2=2$; Green/Stokes annihilates the exact terms.

\section{An elementary bounded all-test estimate}
Let $a,b,w\in\mathcal C$, set $f=a-b$, $g=(a+b)/2$, $h=w-g$, and
\[
 I(a,b)=\int(a-b)(\MA(b)-\MA(a)).
\]
The bounded product expansion gives
\[
 I=Q_{\theta_a}(f,f)+Q_{\theta_b}(f,f)\ge0.
\]
Multilinearity and Green give the signed identity
\[
 Q_{\theta_w}(f,f)-Q_{\theta_g}(f,f)
 =Q_{\theta_a}(f,h)-Q_{\theta_b}(f,h).
\]
Indeed both sides are $-\int f\DD f\wedge\DD h$.
Thus Cauchy--Schwarz implies
\[
 Q_{\theta_w}(f,f)\le I/2+
 \sqrt{I\bigl(Q_{\theta_a}(h,h)+Q_{\theta_b}(h,h)\bigr)}.
\]
For an explicit bounded version choose $B_0$ with
$|a|,|b|,|w|\le B_0$. Then $|h|\le2B_0$, and
\[
 Q_{\theta_a}(h,h)
 =-\int h\,[B(a,w)-(\MA(a)+B(a,b))/2]
 \le4MB_0.
\]
The same holds in the $b$ slot, since every positive measure in the
brackets has mass $M$. Consequently
\[
 Q_{\theta_w}(a-b,a-b)\le I/2+\sqrt{8MB_0I}.
\]
This estimate is sufficient here; it claims no uniform sup-norm bound
for unbounded generated presentations.

\begin{lemma}\label{annihilate}
If $u,v\in\mathcal C$ satisfy $\MA(u)=\MA(v)$ and $d=u-v$, then
$\DD(d\theta_w)=0$ for every $w\in\mathcal C$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Equality of the measures gives $I(u,v)=0$. The estimate gives
$Q_{\theta_w}(d,d)=0$. Cauchy--Schwarz with compact smooth scalar
tests and the Green identity show that every test pairing of
$\DD(d\theta_w)$ vanishes. The difference is bounded and continuous.
\end{proof}

\section{Laurent divisor currents from glued smooth caps}
Take a nonzero Laurent polynomial $A$. At a point of its zero locus
choose an injective chart $|x_i-a_i|<r<1/2$, and put
$\rho_a=|x-a|^2/2$. Choose a smooth convex $\chi$ with
$\chi=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$, $0\le\chi'\le1$, and
$\chi(t)=t-c$ for $t\ge1$. The functions
\[
 \psi_N=\chi(\log|A|+N)
\]
extend smoothly by zero near the zeros of $A$ and are ordinary smooth
psh: away from those zeros $A$ is a unit moment, and at each zero the
cap is locally constant.

Fix $0<\delta<r^2/4$ and choose $\epsilon_N>0$ such that
$\delta+\epsilon_N\sup\psi_N<r^2/2$ on the closed polyannulus.
Then
\[
 w_N=\max(\rho_a,\delta+\epsilon_N\psi_N)-\rho_a
\]
extends by zero to a member of $\mathcal C$. The strict boundary
inequality supplies a collar where it is zero, and smooth soft maxima
give the required locally uniform psh approximation. On the fixed
smaller neighborhood $\rho_a<\delta/2$ one has
$\theta_{w_N}=\epsilon_N\DD\psi_N$. Lemma\ref{annihilate} gives
$\DD(d\DD\psi_N)=0$ there.

CLD16.7.3 applies to the regular holomorphic $A$ on the smooth,
pure-dimensional, boundaryless torus chart:
\[
 \DD[\log|A|]=\delta_{\operatorname{div}A}.
\]
The lower-dimensional support fact used in its immediate proof says
that compact smooth top-degree tests avoid $\{A=0\}$.
On such a test support, $\psi_N-N=\log|A|-c$ for all sufficiently large
$N$. Thus the positive currents $\DD\psi_N$ converge weakly to the
actual divisor current. CLD8.5.1 with the continuous coefficient $d$,
followed by continuous differentiation of currents, proves
\[
 \DD(d\delta_{\operatorname{div}A})=0
\]
on the smaller neighborhood. Covering the divisor proves the local
identity everywhere in every chart; off the divisor it is automatic.
The argument does not assert closedness of $d\delta_{\operatorname{div}A}$.

\section{Rational-domain approximation with controlled denominators}
Here is the neighborhood point needed below. The ordinary topology of
an affinoid spectrum is the initial topology of its absolute-value
functions. Around a point in the interior of a polyannulus, choose
finitely many strict lower and upper bounds defining a neighborhood
contained in the prescribed open set. Move the endpoints slightly
inwards, keeping the point inside. Bounds of the form $|s|^{m/n}$ are
dense among positive real bounds, so every chosen constraint can be
written using an integral power of its function and a scalar in $K$.
Weierstrass upper constraints have denominator one. For the finitely
many positive lower constraints $|h_i|\ge a_i$, use common denominator
$h_0=\prod_i h_i$, numerators $h_0/h_i$, and add numerator one with
the redundant bound $1\le(\prod_i a_i)^{-1}|h_0|$. The added numerator
ensures the unit-ideal condition and excludes every zero of $h_0$;
on its complement the other inequalities are exactly the lower
constraints. Upper constraints multiply their numerators by $h_0$.
This gives a rational domain contained in the chosen neighborhood and
having the point in its ordinary interior. Integral powers realize
the scalar bounds in the ordinary strict presentation when needed.
Thus shrinking to such a compact rational neighborhood is justified
in the ordinary topology, not merely by a rigid admissible cover.

\begin{lemma}\label{rational}
Let $V$ be a rational domain in a compact torus polyannulus $P$, and
$F\in\mathcal O(V)$. There are rational functions
$F_n=A_n/Q_n$, with Laurent-polynomial numerators and denominators,
such that $Q_n$ is a unit on $V$ and $F_n\to F$ uniformly on $V$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write the defining presentation as
\[
 \mathcal O(V)=\mathcal O(P)\langle r_i^{-1}T_i\rangle/
                    (g_0T_i-g_i),
\]
where $g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ generate the unit ideal and the domain is
defined by $|g_i|\le r_i|g_0|$. These inequalities and the unit-ideal
condition imply that $g_0$ has no zero on $V$. It is a unit there and
has a positive lower absolute-value bound by compactness.
Finite polynomials in $T_i$ with coefficients in $\mathcal O(P)$
approximate $F$. Each such expression is a finite sum of products of
the $g_i/g_0$ and finitely many coefficients. Laurent polynomials are
dense in the polyannulus algebra by its completed-series definition.
Approximate these finitely many coefficients and all $g_i$ on $P$.
Choose the approximation $q$ to $g_0$ with
$\|q-g_0\|_V<\inf_V|g_0|$. Then $|q|=|g_0|$ on $V$, and $q$ is a
unit there. Substitution in the fixed finite expression is continuous
in the uniform norm, because inverse denominators have this fixed
positive lower bound. Clearing a finite power of $q$ gives a quotient
$A/q^m$ of Laurent polynomials. Choosing each finite truncation and
its substitutions with error tending to zero proves the assertion.
No uniform bound on the degrees or on the denominator powers is needed.
\end{proof}

\section{All local principal analytic divisor tests}
\begin{theorem}\label{localdiv}
Let $u,v\in\mathcal C$ satisfy $\MA(u)=\MA(v)$, and let $W$ be an
ordinary open subset of a torus chart. For every regular holomorphic
function $F$ on $W$,
\[
 \DD\bigl((u-v)\delta_{\operatorname{div}F}\bigr)=0
                      \quad\text{on }W.
\]
This includes local analytic hypersurfaces not defined by a Laurent
polynomial on the entire torus.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Shrink around any point to the interior of a compact rational domain
$V\subset W$ in a polyannulus. Lemma\ref{rational} gives
$F_n=A_n/Q_n\to F$ uniformly. After omitting initial terms the numerator
is nonzero. A nonzero Laurent polynomial is regular on the smooth
torus, and $Q_n$ is a unit on $V$. Poincare--Lelong therefore gives the
positive current identity on its interior
\[
 T_n=\DD[\log|F_n|]
       =\delta_{\operatorname{div}A_n}.
\]
The preceding section gives $\DD(dT_n)=0$ there, where $d=u-v$.

For any compact smooth $(2,2)$ test $\alpha$ in this interior, its
support avoids the lower-dimensional zero locus of the regular $F$.
Hence $m_\alpha=\inf_{\operatorname{supp}\alpha}|F|>0$. Uniform
approximation implies $|F_n-F|<m_\alpha$ on that support for all late
$n$. The ultrametric inequality gives $|F_n|=|F|$ there. The currents
$[\log|F_n|]$ therefore agree with $[\log|F|]$ on each such test for
all sufficiently late $n$, and converge weakly. Differentiation and
Poincare--Lelong yield
\[
 T_n\longrightarrow\DD[\log|F|]
                          =\delta_{\operatorname{div}F}.
\]
These are positive currents. CLD8.5.1 now gives
$dT_n\to d\delta_{\operatorname{div}F}$, because $d$ is bounded
continuous. Differentiating and using $\DD(dT_n)=0$ proves the result
on the interior of $V$. The local assertions glue on $W$.
\end{proof}
This passage uses approximation on a rational neighborhood and
invertibility of its denominators. It makes no assertion that an
arbitrary analytic curve map has a local closed hypersurface image,
or that the current identity automatically survives every scalar
extension. The weighting step is not licensed for an unbounded
generated difference without a separate integrability theorem.


\section{From a divisor-current identity to a curve Laplacian}
We work first in the torus cover $Y=(\mathbb G_m^2)_K^{\rm an}$.
Let $d$ denote the pullback of the bounded continuous difference $u-v$.
The quotient map is a local analytic isomorphism. The divisor identities
proved above therefore hold on the ordinary open torus atlas of $Y$.

Let $P\in K[T]$ be a nonconstant irreducible polynomial with nonzero
constant term. Characteristic zero makes $P$ separable. The smooth,
reduced principal curve
\[
 C_P=\{P(z_1)=0\}\subset Y
\]
is $\mathbb G_{m,L}^{\rm an}$ viewed as a $K$-analytic space, where
$L=K[T]/(P)$. Its closed immersion $j$ is proper. The divisor current
of $P(z_1)$ is exactly $j_*\delta_{C_P}$, with multiplicity one.
For every chartwise continuous dpsh function $d$, continuous
multiplication and pushforward give
\[
 d\,j_*\delta_{C_P}=j_*((j^*d)\delta_{C_P}),\qquad
 \DD(d\delta_{\operatorname{div}P(z_1)})
       =j_*\DD_{C_P}[j^*d].                 \tag{1}
\]
Here $d$ is locally a difference of continuous psh functions because
the smooth reference potential cancels; pullback preserves this
minimal sheaf. The whole continuous projection-formula argument is
CLD8.5.6, extended by linearity; commutation of pushforward and both
differentials is CLD7.7.8. The same identity follows directly by
testing the weighted integration currents, so it does not require
closedness of a continuously weighted divisor current.

On the curve, $\DD_{C_P}[j^*d]$ is locally a difference of positive
scalar currents and thus a signed Radon measure. A proper closed
embedding pushes such a measure by the ordinary measure pushforward.
That pushforward is injective: a Borel set of the closed subspace is
a Borel subset of the ambient space. CLD7.2.8 identifies signed
Radon measures with their scalar currents, using density of compact
smooth functions. Equation(1) and the preceding divisor identity give
\[
                    \DD_{C_P}[d|_{C_P}]=0.                 \tag{2}
\]
This local conclusion glues along the whole noncompact curve.
The same assertion holds for the horizontal curve $z_2=1$.

There is a normalization to record before using(2) over $L$.
The underlying analytic functions and moment maps on $C_P$ are the
same when it is viewed over $K$ or over $L$. CLD14.4.3 states and
proves that its $K$-calibration is $[L:K]$ times its $L$-calibration.
Consequently the corresponding integration currents and Laplacians
have this same positive factor. Vanishing in(2) therefore gives
vanishing for the $L$-analytic curve with its own normalization.
We do not identify these two calibrations without their factor.

\section{Finite Galois base change of a zero signed Laplacian}
\begin{lemma}\label{finitegalois}
Let $L$ be a complete nontrivially valued field of characteristic zero,
let $E/L$ be a finite Galois extension, and let
$\pi:\mathbb G_{m,E}^{\rm an}\longrightarrow\mathbb G_{m,L}^{\rm an}$
be the base-change map. If $h$ is continuous, locally dpsh, and
$\DD[h]=0$, then $\DD[h\circ\pi]=0$ with the canonical
$E$-analytic normalization.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Pullback preserves continuous psh functions: the assertion holds for
smooth psh generators, pullback preserves locally uniform convergence,
and the inverse-image sheaf minimality proves it at every stage.
Thus $h\circ\pi$ is locally dpsh and
$\mu=\DD[h\circ\pi]$ is a signed Radon measure. It is invariant under
$G=\operatorname{Gal}(E/L)$, since $h\circ\pi$ is invariant and
the isometric automorphisms preserve the canonical calibration.

With the canonical normalization over the varying base field,
CLD15.3.1 and16.1.1 give $\pi_*\delta_{\mathbb G_{m,E}}
=\delta_{\mathbb G_{m,L}}$. Bounded continuous multiplication
locally on a compact test support therefore gives
\[
 \pi_*[h\circ\pi]=[h],\qquad
 \pi_*\mu=\DD\pi_*[h\circ\pi]=\DD[h]=0.        \tag{3}
\]
For clarity, if the source is instead viewed as an $L$-analytic
finite cover, its calibration is multiplied by $[E:L]$ and both
equalities acquire that factor. Either convention proves the same
vanishing. We use the varying-base convention in(3).

Every fibre of $\pi$ is a single $G$-orbit. Indeed it is the spectrum
of the finite etale algebra $\mathscr H(x)\otimes_L E$, a product
of finite field extensions of the complete field $\mathscr H(x)$.
The Galois group permutes its factors transitively: its invariant
algebra is $\mathscr H(x)$, which has no nontrivial idempotent.
Each factor has a unique extending absolute value and contributes
one analytic point. The finite proper surjective map $\pi$ is closed,
hence a topological quotient.

For $\varphi\in C_c(\mathbb G_{m,E}^{\rm an})$ put
$\overline\varphi=|G|^{-1}\sum_{\sigma\in G}\varphi\circ\sigma$.
It is continuous, compactly supported, and constant on each fibre,
so it descends to $\psi\in C_c(\mathbb G_{m,L}^{\rm an})$.
Invariance of $\mu$ and(3), interpreted as signed measures through
CLD7.2.8, imply
\[
 \int\varphi\,d\mu=\int\overline\varphi\,d\mu
                      =\int\psi\,d(\pi_*\mu)=0.
\]
Hence $\mu=0$. This proves only the stated finite Galois passage;
no unrestricted pullback theorem for distributional currents is used.
\end{proof}

\section{Gauss-ray Liouville lemma}
\begin{lemma}\label{liouville}
Let $L$ be a complete nontrivially valued field of characteristic zero.
A bounded continuous locally dpsh function $h$ on
$\mathbb G_{m,L}^{\rm an}$ with $\DD[h]=0$ is constant.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $\eta_{a,r}$ for the Gauss point of the closed disk centred at
$a$ with radius $r>0$; its polynomial norm is
$\left|\sum b_i(z-a)^i\right|=\max_i|b_i|r^i$.
Put $H_0(t)=h(\eta_{0,e^{-t}})$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ the function
$\phi(-\log|z|)$ is smooth with compact support in a closed annulus
inside $\mathbb G_m$. The canonical one-dimensional torus calibration
and integration give
\[
 0=\langle\DD[h],\phi(-\log|z|)\rangle
       =\int_{\mathbb R} H_0(t)\phi''(t)\,dt.       \tag{4}
\]
This is the ordinary calibrated torus moment $z$, of degree one:
$\DD\phi(t)=\phi''(t)d't\wedge d''t$ and its scalar measure is
the pushforward of $\phi''(t)dt$ by the Gauss section. This follows
directly by integrating the one-dimensional calibrated cell; there
is no multiplicity from a larger ground field in the $L$-normalization.
The section and its norm formula are CLD12.1.2,12.1.5.
Equation(4) makes $H_0$ affine as a distribution on $\mathbb R$.
Continuity identifies it with that affine function; boundedness
forces its slope to vanish. Denote its constant value by $c$.

Take $a\in L^*$. On the punctured disk $0<|z-a|<|a|$ the coordinate
$z-a$ is a unit and the disk is contained in $\mathbb G_m$.
The same degree-one annulus calculation, with compact test support,
makes
\[
 H_a(t)=h(\eta_{a,e^{-t}}),\qquad t>-\log|a|,
\]
affine on this half-line. Boundedness as $t\to+\infty$ forces slope
zero. As $r\downarrow0$, $\eta_{a,r}$ converges to the rational
point $a$; this follows from the displayed polynomial norm and the
initial seminorm topology. As $r\uparrow|a|$, it converges to
$\eta_{a,|a|}=\eta_{0,|a|}$. The equality follows by expanding
polynomials at either centre and applying the ultrametric inequality
in both directions. Continuity now gives $h(a)=c$.

A closed rigid point $x$ of $\mathbb G_{m,L}^{\rm an}$ has finite
residue field over $L$. Choose a finite Galois normal closure $E/L$
of that residue field; characteristic zero supplies separability.
Lemma\ref{finitegalois} applies to $h_E=h\circ\pi$. Its Gauss
section at zero projects to the original Gauss section by the norm
formula (also CLD12.1.8(a)). Thus the constant in its Gauss-ray
calculation is the same $c$. A lift of $x$ is an $E$-rational point,
and the previous paragraph proves $h(x)=c$.

We justify the density used to finish the proof. Every nonempty
ordinary open subset of the strict analytic torus contains a
nonempty strict rational affinoid domain: move finite absolute-value
bounds inward while keeping a chosen point inside and replace their
endpoints by elements of $|L^*|^{\mathbb Q}$; that group is dense
since the valuation is nontrivial. Integral powers realize these
constraints with scalars in $L$, using the common-denominator
unit-ideal construction given above. A compact polyannulus containing
the construction can likewise be given a strict presentation by
integral powers. The resulting nonzero strict affinoid algebra has
a maximal ideal. The Tate Nullstellensatz gives a finite residue
extension of $L$, with its unique absolute value, and therefore a
closed rigid analytic point in that domain. Here the Nullstellensatz
is the named ordinary affinoid foundation; Van der Put1.6 records
the exact finite-residue statement, and Papikian3.2(d) corroborates it.
Their short immediate passages do not contain a whole proof of
Weierstrass preparation. No fresh proof of that deeper result is claimed.
Closed rigid points are therefore dense. Since $h$ is continuous and
equals $c$ on them, it is identically $c$.
\end{proof}

\section{Coordinate fibres prove bounded uniqueness}
\begin{theorem}\label{boundedunique}
On the compact analytic quotient specified in the first section, let
$u,v\in\mathcal C$. If their actual recursively defined measures
$\MA(u)$ and $\MA(v)$ agree, then $u-v$ is constant pointwise on $X$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The difference pulled back to $Y$ is bounded and continuous.
Equations(1)--(2) and the calibration comparison show that its
restriction to every vertical $C_P\cong\mathbb G_{m,L}^{\rm an}$
is locally continuous dpsh with zero Laplacian over $L$.
Lemma\ref{liouville} makes each such restriction constant.
The same lemma on the horizontal $K$-curve $z_2=1$ makes its
restriction a single constant $c$ there.

Let $y$ be any closed rigid point of $Y$. Its coordinates have values
$(a,b)$ in a finite extension $E/K$. Let $P$ be the minimal polynomial
of $a$ over $K$ and $L=K(a)$. Then $y$ lies on $C_P$.
The point $(a,1)$ of that curve lies also on $z_2=1$ and has value
$c$. Constancy on $C_P$ therefore gives $d(y)=c$, irrespective of
whether $b$ lies in $L$ or in a larger finite extension. This uses
the entire $L$-analytic curve, not just its $L$-rational points.

Closed rigid points are dense in $Y$ by the same strict rational
domain and Nullstellensatz argument in dimension two.
Continuity gives $d=c$ on all of $Y$. The surjective quotient map
then gives $u-v=c$ on all of $X$.
\end{proof}
The proof of Theorem\ref{boundedunique} needs only the Laurent
divisor tests, although the full local holomorphic divisor extension
has also been retained above. General curve recognition, normalization
of arbitrary curve images, and infinite scalar extension are not
premises of the coordinate-fibre proof.

\documentclass[11pt]{article}

\newcommand{\CPsh}{\operatorname{CPsh}}

\title{Classical recognition, Shilov reconstruction, and upper control\\for generated analytic weights}
\author{Working paper; independent review pending}
\date{9 October 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
We apply the precise classical-psh foundations of Gubler--Rabinoff to the
minimal continuous CLD sheaf and its decreasing generated weights. This
gives tests by all analytic curves after all analytic field extensions,
the local maximum principle, and the affinoid Shilov maximum principle.
We spell out two consequences for an analytic torus quotient: local
weights are reconstructed from finite Shilov boundaries of arbitrarily
small affinoid neighborhoods, and convergence at all such boundary
points implies uniform upper control against a continuous candidate.
These are applications of retained source theorems. We do not claim a new
maximum principle or deduce compactness, envelopes, or the full
Monge--Ampere existence and uniqueness theorem from these consequences.
\end{abstract}

\section{Definitions and the exact source foundations}
Let $K$ be a complete non-Archimedean field and let $V$ be a good
$K$-analytic space. In the application $V$ is an ordinary open chart of
the analytic surface
\[
 K=\mathbb C((s)),\quad |s|=e^{-1/8},\qquad
 X=((\mathbb G_m)^2)^{\mathrm{an}}/
       \langle(s^8,2),(3,s^8)\rangle .
\]
The quotient and nonalgebraization are separate retained geometric
foundations. Here we use only its good open torus atlas. On a chart let
$x_i=-\log|z_i|$ and
\[
 \rho=\tfrac12(x_1^2+x_2^2),\qquad \theta=\DD\rho.
\]
The reference potential changes by an affine function of the unit
logarithms on an overlap.

The sheaf $\CPsh_V$ is the smallest sheaf of finite continuous real
functions containing ordinary CLD smooth functions with positive
$(1,1)$-Hessian and closed under uniform limits. The positivity is the
ordinary positive semidefinite cone in bidegree $(1,1)$.
Let $\mathcal C_\theta$ consist of finite continuous $u$ such that
$\rho+u\in\CPsh_V$ locally. A generated weight is a pointwise decreasing
limit of members of $\mathcal C_\theta$; the finite-energy generated class
adds the stated common lower energy bound. The results below do not need
the energy bound.

We use the exact arXiv:2506.13548v2 snapshot of Gubler--Rabinoff, dated
17 September 2025~\cite{GR}. Its definition of an analytic curve is a
separated analytic space of pure dimension one. Definition3.4 defines
subharmonicity on an arbitrary curve by all pullbacks from connected
smooth strictly analytic curves over nontrivially valued analytic field
extensions. Such a pullback must be either Thuillier-subharmonic or
identically $-\infty$. Thus the extended value is retained without
excluding identically infinite components.

Definition4.1 says that an upper semicontinuous function
$h:V\to[-\infty,\infty)$ is classically psh if, for every analytic
field extension $L/K$, every $L$-analytic curve $C$, and every actual
analytic morphism $f:C\to V_L$, its pullback
$h\circ\pi_{L/K}\circ f$ is subharmonic in Definition3.4. This definition
does not restrict to algebraic curves. Write $\PSH(V)$ for this class.

The following exact source results are retained:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The smooth-psh bridge in Section1.2: ordinary CLD smooth psh
functions are classically psh. The source reduces to smooth curves after
algebraically closed nontrivially valued extension and applies Wanner's
Theorem4.7. We retain this analytic-curve bridge as a named source
foundation. Its recursive local curve, model, and semistable background
is not newly proved here.
\item Proposition4.2: classical psh functions form a sheaf, are closed
under nonnegative linear combinations and finite maxima, and are closed
under infima of decreasing nets. They are compatible with all analytic
field extensions and all actual analytic morphisms. The converse
functorial statement in the source requires finite surjectivity; no such
converse is used below.
\item Theorem6.1: a classically psh function attaining a local maximum
at a point of the relative interior of an analytic space is locally
constant at that point.
\item Theorem6.4: a classically psh function on any $K$-affinoid space
attains its maximum at a Shilov point. The theorem includes possibly
trivially valued $K$ and general affinoid radii.
\end{enumerate}
The local maximum theorem uses the source's Theorem5.4, connectivity by
analytic curves and, for connected boundaryless spaces, by overconvergent
analytic curves. The global affinoid theorem uses its boundary
stratification, Lemma6.3. These are source foundations with their exact
analytic scope, rather than assertions inferred from a catalogue.

\section{Recognition of the whole continuous sheaf}
\begin{lemma}\label{uniform}
The finite continuous classical-psh functions form a sheaf closed under
uniform limits on an open set.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Sheafiness is Proposition4.2(1). Suppose $h_j$ converges uniformly to a
finite continuous $h$. Pass to a subsequence, still denoted $h_j$, with
$\|h_j-h\|_\infty\le2^{-j}$. Define
\[
 g_j=h_j+3\,2^{-j}.
\]
Adding a constant preserves classical psh. Moreover
\[
 g_{j+1}-g_j
 \le 2^{-(j+1)}+2^{-j}-3\,2^{-(j+1)}=0.
\]
Thus $g_j$ decreases pointwise to $h$. Proposition4.2(4) proves that
$h$ is classically psh. For locally uniform limits the same proof is
made on smaller opens and sheafiness glues the conclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{recognition}
Every member of $\CPsh_V$ is classically psh. Every decreasing generated
local weight $\rho+u$ is classically psh, with its extended $-\infty$
values retained. The assertion includes every continuous-sheaf stage,
all analytic curve tests, and all analytic field extensions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Consider the sheaf of finite continuous members of $\PSH$.
The smooth bridge shows that it contains the smooth generators of
$\CPsh$. Lemma\ref{uniform} shows uniform closure.
The defining minimality gives $\CPsh\subset\PSH$ at all stages.
If $u_j\in\mathcal C_\theta$ decreases to $u$, the local functions
$\rho+u_j$ are classically psh and decrease to $\rho+u$.
Apply Proposition4.2(4) and then its field-extension and pullback rules.
\end{proof}
The minimality argument does not identify $\CPsh$ with its first
locally uniformly smooth-approximable stage. It proves one inclusion
into a different sheaf. The underlying classical-psh bridge is already
stated by Gubler--Rabinoff; no novelty is claimed for that bridge.

\begin{corollary}\label{maximum}
A generated local weight satisfies the local maximum principle at
relative interior points and the Shilov maximum principle on every
affinoid domain contained in the chart. In particular, for such a domain
$A$ with finite Shilov boundary $\Gamma_A$,
\[
 \max_{A}(\rho+u)=\max_{\Gamma_A}(\rho+u).
 \tag{1}
\]
If every boundary value is $-\infty$, the local weight is $-\infty$
throughout $A$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorem\ref{recognition} and the exact source Theorems6.1 and6.4 apply.
Restriction to an affinoid domain is an actual analytic morphism, so
Proposition4.2(6) justifies that restriction. Upper semicontinuity gives
the maximum on compact $A$; the source theorem places it in $\Gamma_A$.
The case of an identically infinite function is allowed by its definition.
\end{proof}
It is $\rho+u$, rather than $u$ alone, that obeys (1). The reference
potential must remain in the boundary values.

\section{Reconstruction from arbitrarily small finite boundaries}
For a point $x\in V$, write $\mathcal A_x(V)$ for the affinoid
neighborhoods of $x$ contained in $V$, with $x$ in their ordinary
topological interior. The standard neighborhood property of good
analytic spaces supplies such a neighborhood inside every ordinary
open neighborhood of $x$. Let
\[
 D(V)=\bigcup_{A\subset V\text{ affinoid}}\Gamma_A.
\]
The boundaries in this union vary with $A$; this is not one fixed finite
set or one prescribed skeleton.

\begin{theorem}\label{reconstruction}
For every classically psh $q:V\to[-\infty,\infty)$,
\[
 q(x)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_x(V)}\ \max_{\xi\in\Gamma_A}q(\xi).
 \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, for every generated weight on a chart,
\[
 u(x)=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_x(V)}
       \max_{\xi\in\Gamma_A}\bigl(\rho(\xi)+u(\xi)\bigr)-\rho(x).
 \tag{3}
\]
All these identities retain points where the weight is $-\infty$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each $A$ the Shilov maximum theorem gives
$q(x)\le\max_{\Gamma_A}q$. This is one inequality in (2).
If $q(x)$ is finite, for any $\epsilon>0$ upper semicontinuity gives an
ordinary open neighborhood $O$ of $x$ on which $q<q(x)+\epsilon$.
Choose $A\in\mathcal A_x(V)$ contained in $O$. Then
$\max_{\Gamma_A}q\le q(x)+\epsilon$.
Take the infimum and let $\epsilon$ decrease to zero.
If $q(x)=-\infty$, upper semicontinuity gives such an $O$ with
$q<B$ for every prescribed real $B$. The same argument shows that the
infimum is at most every $B$, hence is $-\infty$.
Apply (2) to $q=\rho+u$ to obtain (3).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{order}
For classical-psh $q,r$ on $V$, if $q\le r$ on $D(V)$ then $q\le r$
on $V$. For two generated weights with the same reference potential,
their order, and hence equality, is determined by their values on
$D(V)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For each affinoid $A$ the assumed inequality on $\Gamma_A$ gives
$\max_{\Gamma_A}q\le\max_{\Gamma_A}r$.
Take infima in (2). For weights apply this to $\rho+u$ and $\rho+v$.
\end{proof}
Every nonempty ordinary open contains a nonempty affinoid domain, whose
Shilov boundary is nonempty. Thus $D(V)$ is dense. Nevertheless
Corollary\ref{order} is not merely the determination of a continuous
function by dense values: the weights may be discontinuous or have poles,
and (2) provides the needed upper-semicontinuous reconstruction.

\section{Upper control near a continuous candidate}
\begin{theorem}\label{Hartogs}
Let $(q_j)$ be a net of classical-psh functions on the good space $V$.
Let $h$ be a finite continuous real function on $V$, and assume
\[
 \limsup_j q_j(\xi)\le h(\xi)\qquad\text{for every }\xi\in D(V).
 \tag{4}
\]
Then, for every compact $Q\subset V$ and every $\epsilon>0$,
$q_j\le h+\epsilon$ on $Q$ for all sufficiently large $j$.
In particular
\[
 \limsup_j\sup_Q(q_j-h)\le0.
 \tag{5}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Fix $\eta>0$. For each $x\in Q$ choose an affinoid neighborhood $A_x$
contained in $V$ on which the oscillation of $h$ is less than $\eta$.
This is possible by continuity and goodness. Finitely many ordinary
interiors of these neighborhoods cover $Q$; write them $A_1,\ldots,A_m$.
Their Shilov boundaries have finite union. By (4), a common late index
gives $q_j(\xi)\le h(\xi)+\eta$ at every point of that finite union.
For $y\in Q\cap A_i$, the affinoid maximum principle now gives
\[
 q_j(y)\le\max_{\Gamma_{A_i}}q_j
 \le\max_{\Gamma_{A_i}}h+\eta
 \le h(y)+2\eta.
\]
The common late index exists for a net because its index set is directed.
Take $2\eta<\epsilon$ to obtain the assertion and then (5).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{weighted}
Let $(u_j)$ be generated $\theta$-psh weights on the compact quotient
$X$, and let $f$ be finite continuous. Suppose that on every reference
chart the boundary-value condition
$\limsup_j u_j(\xi)\le f(\xi)$ holds at all its affinoid Shilov points.
Then $u_j\le f+\epsilon$ on $X$ for every $\epsilon>0$ and every
sufficiently late $j$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
On each chart apply Theorem\ref{Hartogs} to $q_j=\rho+u_j$ and
$h=\rho+f$. Compactness and the good open atlas give a finite collection
of compact affinoid neighborhoods contained in the charts and covering
$X$. Apply the theorem on these compact sets and take a common late
index. Subtract the corresponding reference potential on each chart.
\end{proof}
This conclusion controls only the upper errors. It neither asserts
uniform convergence nor bounds the negative tails of an energy sublevel.

\section{The remaining compactness and equation gates}
Equations (2)--(5) replace a previously missing maximum and determination
input for the full generated class. The ordinary analytic Shilov points
here are not an invariant-measure support restriction. A Monge--Ampere
measure is not assigned by these boundary evaluations.

These facts still do not supply a compactness theorem for normalized
finite-energy potentials. A limit of their values on $D(V)$ need not
already be the boundary values of a generated weight. Nor is an arbitrary
pointwise limit automatically upper semicontinuous. The exact source
Theorem6.5 assumes that a pointwise net limit is upper semicontinuous
before concluding it is classical psh; it cannot remove this requirement.
Reconstruction from genuine psh values in (2) is not a construction of
every prescribed boundary-value limit.

No converse identification with all intrinsic psh weights, continuous
obstacle envelope theorem, orthogonality, uniform integrability of all
finite-dual measures on energy sublevels, arbitrary-support equation
existence, or full uniqueness follows here. Original P16.7 remains open.
The proposed applications and this working paper await independent review.

\section{Source version and audit boundary}
The complete applied definitions and immediate proofs in the retained
Gubler--Rabinoff v2 text were read for Proposition4.2 and
Theorems5.4,6.1,6.4,6.5, together with the actual boundary stratification
Lemma6.3 and the relevant curve maximum, base-change, and sheaf proofs.
The exact smooth bridge is stated and argued in Section1.2.
The recursive Berkovich, Ducros, Temkin, Thuillier, and Wanner proof trees
remain named source foundations, not entire freshly audited proof trees.
In particular we use no unsupported arbitrary-current pullback.

The actual original PDF pages3,33,34 were also inspected. Page3 contains
the analytic-curve bridge, and pages33--34 contain the full statement and
immediate proof of Theorem6.4 and the pointwise-limit theorem.
The extracted and printed proof of Theorem6.4 says ``since $h$ is continuous'' when
claiming that the maximum set is closed. The theorem's stated hypothesis
is upper semicontinuity; at the attained supremum that condition already
makes the maximum set closed. Our proofs use exactly upper
semicontinuity. The literal source text is retained without silently
altering its words. The snapshot is not identified byte for byte with
any later publication, and no complete new reading of the entire paper
or of its recursive dependencies is claimed.

\title{Bounded atomic tests at all full-dimensional analytic points\\
Pointwise lower bounds for genuinely generated finite-energy weights}
\author{Research working paper 402; unreviewed}
\date{9 October 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
On the actual nonalgebraic analytic torus quotient over
$\mathbb C((s))$, every point of graded dimension two is a positive
atom of the actual Monge--Ampere measure of a globally glued bounded
continuous test potential. The construction uses Laurent polynomial
Abhyankar moments, arbitrary real Gauss radii, a finite flat local
map, and the raw calibrated mass of a log-maximum. It requires no
change of ground field. The full bounded energy dual then implies
finiteness of every genuinely decreasing-generated finite-energy
weight at every such point, with a uniform lower bound on each
normalized energy sublevel. In particular all affinoid Shilov values
are finite and uniformly bounded on a fixed sublevel. Product
compactness of these values is separated from actual
representability and energy-sublevel compactness. Full original
P16.7 remains open. All new claims are unreviewed.
\end{abstract}

\section{The actual analytic object and proof foundations}
Put $K=\mathbb C((s))$, $|s|=e^{-1/8}$, $t=s^8$,
$Y=(\mathbb G_m^2)^{\mathrm{an}}_K$, and
\[
 X=Y/\langle(t,2),(3,t)\rangle,\qquad
 \tau=(-\log|z_1|,-\log|z_2|).
\]
The translations on $\tau$ form $\mathbb Z^2$. Ordinary open tropical
boxes of width less than one give injective quotient charts. We use
the previously reconstructed analytic quotient: compact, separated,
good, boundaryless, connected, smooth, and pure of dimension two.
The quotient construction and its nonalgebraization proof are not
reproved here and are not consequences of the present point test.
On a chart let $\rho=|\tau|^2/2$ and $\theta=\DD\rho$.
Changes of reference are affine unit logarithms. With the identity
torus's saturated lattice and degree one,
\[
 M=\int_X\theta^2=2.
\]
This is the raw CLD convention; no probability normalization is made.

Let $\mathscr P$ be the minimal continuous CLD psh sheaf containing
the ordinary smooth psh functions and closed under local uniform
limits. All stages of this sheaf are retained. Set
\[
 \C=\{a\in C(X,\RR):\rho+a\in\mathscr P\text{ locally}\},\quad
 \theta_a=\theta+\DD a,\quad B(a,b)=\theta_a\wedge\theta_b.
\]
We use the actual recursive continuous products. Their positivity,
symmetry, closedness, locality, local uniform continuity, and
invariance under smooth $\DD$-null reference changes are precisely
CLDv2 8.5.1, 8.5.3, 8.5.5--6, 8.7.1--4 and 8.8.4--5, at the stated
continuous psh/dpsh and positive closed-current hypotheses. Positive
top currents are Radon measures by 7.2.8 on these locally
differentially separated charts. Smooth cutoffs, partitions, scalar
approximation and boundaryless Stokes are the conventional analytic
foundations. Arbitrary continuous-multiplier closedness in 8.6.7 is
not a premise. No first-stage identity for $\mathscr P$ is assumed.

Constants, convex combinations and finite maxima preserve $\C$.
For a smooth slot, convex regularized maxima are smooth psh.
Uniform continuity and sheaf minimality extend the operation one
slot at a time to all stages. This also proves ordinary convex
composition with finite continuous psh slots by the same argument.

\section{Bounded Green calculus and the full bounded dual}
Here we give the extra energy argument rather than infer it from
a positivity label. For a positive closed $(1,1)$ current $T$,
complete compact smooth $(1,0)$ forms modulo the null space of
\[
 (a,b)\longmapsto\int a\wedge Jb\wedge T.
\]
Use a nonnegative compact smooth cutoff $\chi$ for the corresponding
local seminorm $Q_{T,\chi}$. Let $\HH_T$ consist of continuous
functions locally uniformly approximable by smooth functions whose
gradients converge strongly in these seminorms. The gradient is
unique: for a uniformly zero sequence $f_j$ with a strong gradient
limit and a compact smooth form $b$, closedness gives
\[
 \int d'f_j\wedge Jb\wedge T=-\int f_jd'(Jb)\wedge T\longrightarrow0.
\]
The right-hand coefficient measure is finite on the fixed compact
support; smooth Hilbert tests are dense. The limit gradient is zero.
Partitions patch local approximants by the Leibniz rule.
Bounded continuous coefficients act by scalar approximation and the
bound $\|fa\|\le\|f\|_\infty\|a\|$. Products and cutoffs have their
usual gradient rules.

If $f\in\HH_T$ and $L_Tf=\DD(fT)$ is signed Radon, smooth
approximation first in $f$, then uniformly and strongly in a
compactly supported $g$, yields
\[
 \int gL_Tf=-Q_T(f,g),\qquad
 Q_{T,\chi}(w,w)=\frac12\int w^2\DD\chi\wedge T-\int\chi wL_Tw.
\]
The sheaf of $f\in\HH_T$ with $L_Tf\ge0$ contains smooth psh
functions and is uniformly closed. Indeed take nested cutoffs
$\chi,\eta$, $\eta=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$,
a common bound $|f_j|\le B$ on the whole support of $\eta$, and
$\epsilon=\|f_j-f_k\|$ there. Positivity and the preceding identity give
\[
 0\le Q_{T,\chi}(f_j-f_k,f_j-f_k)
 \le\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\|\DD\chi\wedge T\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 +2B\epsilon\|\chi\|_\infty\|\DD\eta\wedge T\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]
Choose smooth approximants to $f_j$ with uniform and smaller-patch
gradient errors below $1/j$. The estimate proves strong convergence;
distributional positivity survives. Minimality places every stage
of $\mathscr P$ in this sheaf. Its vector span includes continuous
dpsh functions. Finite patching on compact $X$ proves
\[
 \int f\DD(gT)=\int g\DD(fT)=-Q_T(f,g),\qquad Q_T(f,f)\ge0.
\]
In particular all the following computations hold at every
continuous stage. The exact terms in the bounded product expansion
have zero total integral, so every $B(a,b)$ has mass $M=2$.

Define
\[
 E(a)=\frac13\int_X a[\theta^2+\theta_a\wedge\theta+\theta_a^2].
\]
For $a_t=(1-t)a+tb$, the cubic expansion and Green give
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}E(a_t)=\int(b-a)\MA(a_t),\qquad
 \frac{d^2}{dt^2}E(a_t)=-2Q_{\theta_{a_t}}(b-a,b-a)\le0.
\]
Thus $E$ is concave and monotone, $E(0)=0$, and
$E(a+c)=E(a)+Mc$. Its tangent inequality is
\[
 E(a)\le E(w)+\int(a-w)\MA(w)\qquad(a,w\in\C).
\]
For a positive Radon measure $\mu$ define the \emph{full} bounded dual
\[
 E^*(\mu)=\sup_{a\in\C}\left(E(a)-\int a\,d\mu\right).
\]
Constants force $\mu(X)=M$ whenever this quantity is finite.
The tangent inequality, with equality at $a=w$, proves the exact
formula
\begin{equation}\label{dual}
 E^*(\MA(w))=E(w)-\int w\MA(w)<\infty
 \quad\text{for every }w\in\C.
\end{equation}
It is nonnegative, since $a=0$ is one of the competitors.

\section{The actual generated class and a moment bound}
Let $\G$ consist of actual pointwise limits
$a_j\downarrow u$ on $X$, where $a_j\in\C$ and
$\inf_jE(a_j)>-\infty$. These limits are USC.
They are not abstract functionals or equivalence classes modulo
null sets. Define $E(u)=\lim_jE(a_j)$.
This is independent of every continuous decreasing presentation.
To see this, if $b_k\downarrow u$ and $a$ is continuous with $u<a$
everywhere, the increasing ordinary open sets $\{b_k<a\}$ cover
compact $X$. One index therefore works everywhere. Apply this to
$a=a_j+\epsilon$, use monotonicity and the constant rule, and
then reverse the roles of the presentations. The limits agree.
In particular $E(u)>-\infty$ for every presentation of a member
of $\G$. The identically $-\infty$ limit is excluded: compact
strict domination would eventually put a presentation below every
negative constant, contradicting its energy lower bound.

\begin{lemma}\label{moment}
If $u\in\G$, $u\le0$, and $E^*(\mu)<\infty$ for a positive
Radon measure $\mu$, then
\[
 \int(-u)\,d\mu\le E^*(\mu)-E(u)<\infty.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every term of a presentation satisfies
$\int(-a_j)\,d\mu\le E^*(\mu)-E(a_j)$.
The continuous first term bounds all terms above. Apply monotone
convergence to that common bound minus $a_j$ and pass to the limit.
This proves the claim even at poles and does not presume
integrability before the bound. The same argument proves
$L^1(\mu)$ convergence of the whole presentation.
\end{proof}

\section{Laurent Abhyankar moments without changing the field}
Write $d_K(x)=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\widetilde K}
\widetilde{\mathscr H(x)}$, with graded residue fields.
Let $\mathscr A$ be the set of points of $X$ with $d_K(x)=2$.
A lift of such a point in $Y$ will also be denoted $x$.

\begin{lemma}\label{moments}
There are two nonzero Laurent polynomials $P_1,P_2$ over $K$
whose initial forms at $x$ are algebraically independent over
$\widetilde K$. Put $r_i=|P_i(x)|>0$. Then
\[
 (P_1,P_2)(x)=\eta_{(r_1,r_2)}
\]
in $(\mathbb A_K^2)^{\mathrm{an}}$. The map is finite and flat at
$x$, and admits a local finite flat representative with a positive
constant degree $D$ and with $x$ the only point above this Gauss point.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The support of $x$ on the Laurent polynomial ring is zero.
Otherwise it lies on a proper algebraic subvariety of dimension
at most one, contradicting $d_K(x)=2$ and the Abhyankar inequality.
Thus $\mathscr H(x)$ is the completion of the valued field
$K(z_1,z_2)$. Completion does not add graded residue elements:
approximate a nonzero element with error strictly less than its
norm. Its initial form agrees with that of the approximant.
Consequently the initial forms of all nonzero Laurent polynomials
generate the graded residue \emph{field}, allowing ratios.
A maximal algebraically independent subfamily of these homogeneous
generators has cardinal two. Choosing its members gives $P_1,P_2$.

For every polynomial $\sum_I c_IP^I$, the initial terms of maximal
norm cannot cancel by graded algebraic independence. Its norm is
$\max_I|c_I|r^I$. This is exactly the Gauss seminorm, for arbitrary
real $r_i>0$; no scaling of $r_i$ into $|K^\times|$ is required.
This is also the Abhyankar-basis criterion of CLD 13.8.5.

The torus is boundaryless, hence $x$ is in the relative interior
of the map to $\mathbb A^2$. The target is reduced and the Gauss
point has graded dimension two. CLD 11.6.5(c) makes the map finite
and flat at $x$. Its 11.6.3 local representative can be chosen
with a single point of that fibre. The rank is a positive integer
$D$. After shrinking the target inside its ordinary interior,
the source is an ordinary open neighborhood of $x$, and the finite
flat degree remains $D$ there.
\end{proof}

\section{The actual atomic mass and its global test}
We spell out the local calibrated number.
On a real two-plane set $g(t)=\max(0,t_1,t_2)$ and
$g_\epsilon=\epsilon\log(1+e^{t_1/\epsilon}+e^{t_2/\epsilon})$.
For $g_1$, write $p_i=e^{t_i}/(1+e^{t_1}+e^{t_2})$ and
$p_0=1-p_1-p_2$. The Hessian determinant is $p_0p_1p_2$.
The gradient maps the plane diffeomorphically to
$\{p_1,p_2>0:p_1+p_2<1\}$ with that Jacobian.
The raw superform rule is $2!\det(\operatorname{Hess}g_1)\,dt_1dt_2$.
Its integral is $2!\,(1/2)=1$.
Dilation and dominated convergence concentrate this finite measure
at the origin as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, so
\[
 (\DD g)^2=\delta_0.
\]
This is the explicit case of CLD 1.7.1 and 1.7.6--8, including
their factor $2!$.

Near $x$, both $P_i$ are invertible. Apply the pleasant moment
$(P_1,P_2)$ there. Finite flatness and the single Gauss fibre imply
full tropical dimension and that the calibrated tropical cone at
$x$ is the whole real plane with multiplicity $D$.
Indeed the map is open, so the Gauss section of a neighborhood of
the target gives a neighborhood in the tropical plane. The explicit
calibration formula CLD 14.5.2--3 makes its image calibration
$D$ times the standard one. Locality removes other fibre points,
since there are none in this representative. More explicitly,
smooth log-sum-exp approximants have top measures strongly
supported on the inverse image of the target Gauss section.
The calibrated integration formula pushes them to $D$ times the
corresponding real-plane measures near the target tropical value.
Those measures concentrate there with mass one. Finite properness
and the single Gauss fibre imply that every inverse Gauss point
over a sufficiently small tropical neighborhood lies in any
prescribed ordinary neighborhood of $x$: otherwise compactness
would give another point of that fibre. Continuous tests therefore
converge to $D$ times evaluation at $x$. Local uniform continuity
of the actual product identifies the limit with the log-maximum
product. This reconstructs the atomic calculation 8.9.2--4 and yields
\begin{equation}\label{localatom}
 \left(\DD\max(0,\log(|P_1|/r_1),\log(|P_2|/r_2))\right)^2
 =D\delta_x
 \quad\text{on some ordinary neighborhood of }x.
\end{equation}
Formula \eqref{localatom} uses the normalized
canonical calibration over the unchanged field $K$ and the actual
finite flat degree. No arbitrary-current pullback is invoked.
CLD 18.6.2 gives the equivalent Gauss-fibre description, but its
relative-intersection proof is not needed for this argument.

\begin{theorem}\label{atom}
For every $x\in\mathscr A$ there is $w_x\in\C$ and
$\alpha_x>0$ such that the actual positive Radon measure
$\MA(w_x)$ satisfies
\[
 \MA(w_x)(\{x\})=\alpha_x.
\]
One can take $\alpha_x=\varepsilon^2D$ in the construction below.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose an injective lift chart around the tropical class
$a=\tau(x)$ and a small Euclidean tropical ball of radius $R$ there.
Its inverse image has compact closure inside a polyannulus.
Set $\rho_a=|\tau-a|^2/2$; its difference from $\rho$ is
smooth affine and $\DD$-null.
The function
\[
 \psi=\max(0,\log(|P_1|/r_1),\log(|P_2|/r_2))
\]
is finite, continuous, nonnegative and psh on this whole chart,
including zeros of the polynomials. Here is a direct check at all
continuous stages. Choose a smooth convex $\chi$ equal to zero for
$v\le0$, with $0\le\chi'\le1$, and equal to $v-c$ for $v\ge1$,
where $0<c<1$. For $N>3$ the finite smooth psh function
\[
 p_{i,N}=\chi(\log(|P_i|/r_i)+N)-N+c
\]
is locally constant at zeros. Where it can be positive it equals
$\log(|P_i|/r_i)$, so $\psi=\max(0,p_{1,N},p_{2,N})$ exactly.
Smooth convex regularized maxima place it in $\mathscr P$.

Take $0<\delta<R^2/4$ and choose $\varepsilon>0$ so small that
$\delta+\varepsilon\sup\psi<R^2/2$ on the compact closure.
Then
\[
 w_x=\max(\rho_a,\delta+\varepsilon\psi)-\rho_a
\]
vanishes on a tropical boundary collar. Extend it by zero to $X$.
It belongs to $\C$: regularize the inner finite maximum, and then
use a smooth convex regularized outer maximum which agrees exactly
with the larger slot when the gap exceeds its regularization
width. The fixed collar gap ensures that each sufficiently small
regularization extends by zero smoothly and $\theta$-psh.
Their uniform limit is the displayed function.

On the fixed inner neighborhood $\rho_a<\delta/2$ we have
$\theta_{w_x}=\varepsilon\DD\psi$. Shrink further to the
neighborhood in \eqref{localatom}. Locality of the actual recursive
product gives
$\MA(w_x)=\varepsilon^2D\delta_x$ there.
Outside it the global product remains positive and has raw mass
$M=2$. Thus its atom at $x$ is precisely the positive number
$\alpha_x=\varepsilon^2D$.
\end{proof}

\section{Finiteness, sublevel bounds, and the precise compactness limit}
\begin{corollary}\label{finite}
For every $u\in\G$ and every $x\in\mathscr A$, $u(x)$ is finite.
More precisely, if $\sup_Xu=0$ and $E(u)\ge-C$, then
\[
 -\frac{E^*(\MA(w_x))+C}{\alpha_x}\le u(x)\le0 .
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use \eqref{dual} and Lemma \ref{moment} for the \emph{whole}
positive measure $\mu_x=\MA(w_x)$.
Since $-u\ge0$ and $\mu_x$ contains the positive atom
$\alpha_x\delta_x$,
\[
 \alpha_x(-u(x))\le\int(-u)\,d\mu_x
 \le E^*(\mu_x)-E(u)\le E^*(\mu_x)+C.
\]
This excludes a pole at $x$ and proves the bound.
An arbitrary $u$ can be shifted by its finite supremum.
A member of $\G$ has a finite upper bound and is not identically
$-\infty$, so that shift is legitimate.
\end{proof}

Every Shilov point of a pure-dimensional two-dimensional affinoid
domain in a local chart has $d_K=2$. At the exact general-radius
hypotheses, GRv2 Lemma6.3(3)--(4) expresses these Shilov points as
the strata with two graded algebraically independent generators;
the Abhyankar inequality gives the reverse bound.
The entire lemma and its immediate proof were read, including its
Temkin graded-reduction and Ducros fibre-dimension foundations.
These deeper theorems are named published foundations, not freshly
recursively reproved here. Hence Corollary \ref{finite} applies to
every such Shilov point, not only to the reference torus skeleton.
On a fixed finite Shilov boundary the lower bound can be chosen
uniformly by taking the maximum of the finitely many displayed
constants.

For clarity, actual local weights are classically psh at all
stages. The published smooth CLD-to-classical bridge is the
unnumbered statement and argument in GRv2 Section1.2.
Its Proposition4.2 gives sheafiness and decreasing-net
closure. A uniform limit of finite continuous classical psh
functions is classical psh: select errors at most $2^{-j}$ and add
$3\cdot2^{-j}$, obtaining a decreasing sequence with the same limit.
Sheaf minimality then recognizes all of $\mathscr P$, and a
continuous decreasing presentation recognizes $\rho+u$ at poles.
GRv2 Theorem6.4 therefore gives the affinoid Shilov maximum
principle for these actual USC weights.
For all arbitrarily small affinoid neighborhoods $A$ in one chart,
\[
 (\rho+u)(y)=\inf_{A\ni y\ \mathrm{neighborhood}}
                \max_{\xi\in\Gamma_A}(\rho+u)(\xi).
\]
The maximum principle gives one inequality. USC gives the other
by every finite upper bound at a pole and by
$(\rho+u)(y)+\eta$ at a finite value. Thus values on the union
$\mathscr S$ of \emph{all} these Shilov boundaries determine the
actual weight, including all poles.

Fix a normalized energy sublevel
$\G_C=\{u\in\G:\sup u=0,\ E(u)\ge-C\}$.
Its evaluation map on $\mathscr S$ is injective and takes values in
\[
 \prod_{\xi\in\mathscr S}[-L_\xi(C),0],\qquad
 L_\xi(C)=\frac{E^*(\MA(w_\xi))+C}{\alpha_\xi}.
\]
Tychonoff compactness implies that every net of such evaluations
has a coordinatewise convergent subnet with finite coordinates.
This is compactness in the product space of boundary values.
It does \emph{not} show that the limit coordinates are represented
by an actual member of $\G$, that the normalized image is closed,
or that energy is semicontinuous there. Those are still mathematical
gates for actual energy-sublevel compactness.
Likewise this point bound alone does not prove uniqueness from
equality of generated MA measures.

\begin{remark}
We have not claimed that $\delta_x$ itself has finite full bounded
dual merely because it is part of $\MA(w_x)$.
The whole test measure has the supporting-energy formula
\eqref{dual}; its positivity is exactly what gives the atomic
point inequality. The distinction retains the raw mass-two dual
and avoids an invalid componentwise assertion.
\end{remark}
